titulo: The financial cycle and macroeconomics: what have we learnt?
texto:
The financial cycle and macroeconomics: what have we learnt?

It is high time we rediscovered the role of the financial cycle in macroeconomics. In the environment that has prevailed for at least three decades now, it is not possible to understand business fluctuations and the corresponding analytical and policy challenges without understanding the financial cycle. This calls for a rethink of modelling strategies and for significant adjustments to macroeconomic policies. This essay highlights the stylised empirical features of the financial cycle, conjectures as to what it may take to model it satisfactorily, and considers its policy implications. In the discussion of policy, the essay pays special attention to the bust phase, which is less well explored and raises much more controversial issues.

Authors

Former Head of the Monetary and Economic Department

titulo: Stop believing in haircuts - at least the way you think about them

texto:
Working Paper Series 
Stop believing in haircuts - at least the 
way you think about them 
 
Benedikt Ballensiefen, Jasper Knyphausen, 
Benoît Nguyen 
Disclaimer: This paper should not be reported as representing the views of the European Central Bank 
(ECB). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the ECB.  
No 3301 / October 2026 

Abstract
We study how frictions impact haircut setting in repo markets. Using transaction-level super-
visory data and exploiting the 2021 introduction of the  binding leverage ratio requirement, 
we show that three frictions jointly shape haircuts in the bilateral dealer-to-client segment: 
dealer balance sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. In 
collateral-driven repos, binding leverage constraints and broader client outside options both 
raise haircuts, while higher convenience yields push them down. In funding-driven trades, 
the leverage constraint has no effect, higher convenience yields raise haircuts through the 
rehypothecation channel, and broader client outside options lower them. We rationalise these 
patterns in a bilateral bargaining model with periodic haircut renegotiation. Consistent with 
the model, constrained dealers exhibit higher repo-rate volatility and weaker pass-through 
of ECB policy rate  changes in the collateral-driven segment. Post-crisis bank regulation thus 
carries potential unintended consequences for repo market functioning and the transmission 
of monetary policy.
J.E.L. classification: C78, E43, E52, E58, G12, G21, G28.
Keywords: Bilateral repo, haircuts, dealer balance sheet, convenience yield, client outside options, 
leverage ratio, monetary policy pass-through.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
1

Non-technical Summary
Repo is the largest segment of money markets: cash is borrowed against securities pledged as
collateral, most often government bonds. Market participants use repo either to obtain cash
(funding-driven repos) or to borrow specific securities (collateral-driven repos). In both cases,
the haircut — the difference between the value of the collateral and the cash exchanged — is
commonly viewed as a risk-management tool. It should be positive when a dealer lends cash,
protecting it against having to sell the collateral at a loss if the client defaults, and negative
when a dealer lends a security, protecting it against having to buy the security back at a
higher price if it is not returned. In practice, haircuts in bilateral repo are mostly zero and
often carry the opposite sign. This paper asks what explains these patterns.
Using transaction-level data on euro area bilateral dealer-to-client repos from 2019 to 2024,
we show that haircuts are shaped by three frictions. First, dealer balance-sheet constraints
matter. The Basel III leverage ratio makes it costly for dealers to receive cash in collateral-
driven repos, so dealers closer to their regulatory minimum set higher haircuts in these trades.
This effect emerges once the leverage ratio becomes binding in June 2021, is present through-
out the quarter rather than only at reporting dates, and is absent in funding-driven repos,
which do not expand the dealer’s balance sheet in the same way. Second, the convenience
yield of the collateral matters. Scarce, highly valued government bonds lower haircuts in
collateral-driven trades, where dealers seek protection against the cost of replacing them,
but raise haircuts in funding-driven trades, where dealers can re-use the bonds they receive.
Third, clients’ outside options matter as clients with more dealer relationships obtain more
favourable haircut terms.
A bargaining model between dealer and client rationalises these findings. It recovers the
textbook risk-management haircuts when the frictions are absent and shows that zero and
opposite-sign haircuts are equilibrium outcomes once regulation, collateral scarcity and client
bargaining positions are taken into account. Consistent with the model, leverage-constrained
dealers exhibit more volatile repo rates and pass changes in the ECB’s deposit facility rate
through to their clients less completely in collateral-driven trades. Post-crisis bank regulation
therefore has consequences not only for repo contract terms but also for the transmission of
monetary policy in the repo market.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
2

1. Introduction
Repurchase agreements (repo) — short-term loans secured by securities pledged as collat-
eral, most often government bonds — are the main segment of the money market and play a
central role in the efficient allocation of short-term funding, securities financing, and circula-
tion of collateral. A deep and well-functioning repo market allows financial intermediaries to
manage liquidity, enables non-bank financial institutions to finance leveraged portfolios, and
as the largest segment of the money market is an essential step to transmit monetary policy
to the broader financial system. Given its importance for market efficiency, financial stability,
and the real economy, understanding the frictions that arise in the repo market — and the
mechanisms through which they shape market outcomes — is essential.
Haircuts applied to the collateral leg of repo transactions are generally assumed to be a key
risk-management tool. Yet a growing body of evidence documents that haircuts in bilateral
repo are systematically at zero or even negative across major jurisdictions — Europe (Hermes,
Schmeling, and Schrimpf, 2025a,b; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), the United States (Hempel,
Kahn, Mann, and Paddrik, 2023; Bejarano, Lu, and Wallen, 2025; Kahn and McCormick, 2025;
Cenicola, Mann, and Paddrik, 2025), and the United Kingdom (Julliard, Pinter, Todorov, and
Yuan, 2026). This pattern has revived the policy debate over the financial-stability risks posed
by repo and the associated leverage of non-bank financial institutions, and has led the Fi-
nancial Stability Board to propose, for instance, the imposition of minimum haircut floors
(Financial Stability Board, 2025; Grill, Hermes, and Wedow, 2025). This paper identifies three
money-market frictions — dealer balance-sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and
client outside options — that jointly determine haircut design in bilateral repo markets, and
analyses what these design choices imply for funding conditions, monetary policy transmis-
sion, and financial stability.
In our analysis, we focus on the bilateral dealer-to-client segment of the repo market
where haircuts are the result of a negotiation between the dealer bank and a client such
as a hedge fund. 1 Repos serve a dual purpose in either providing cash or collateral. We
1By contrast, transactions in the inter-dealer segment tend to be centrally cleared with standardized haircuts.
Because dealers have access to a centrally cleared interdealer market—offering capital netting benefits, anonymous
centralized trading, homogeneous counterparty risk, and efficient price discovery—we assume that most trades
in the dealer-to-client segment are client-initiated.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
3

classify transactions in which a dealer provides cash to a client as funding-driven and those in
which a dealer provides collateral as collateral-driven. The haircut is defined as the percentage
difference between the market value of the collateral pledged and the cash lent. The basic
intuition behind collateralised lending is that haircuts should protect the cash- or collateral-
lender from the counterparty’s default, and that rates are a function of supply and demand
for cash and scarce collateral. If a dealer lends out cash (in a funding-driven transaction),
we would expect haircuts to be positive to protect the dealer against a borrower default; if
the borrower defaults, the dealer must sell the collateral at a potentially lower price than at
inception. We refer to this risk as liquidation risk. By contrast, if a dealer lends out collateral
(in a collateral-driven transaction), we would expect haircuts to be negative to protect dealers
against the risk of the collateral not being returned. If the collateral is not returned, the dealer
must re-source it in the market at a potentially higher price. We refer to this risk asreplacement
risk.2
For our empirical analysis, we exploit the ECB’s Money Market Statistical Reporting
(MMSR), a confidential supervisory database of the transaction-level activity of the largest
dealer banks in the euro-area money market. MMSR offers an exceptionally rich window
into the bilateral repo market: for each transaction we observe both counterparties, the spe-
cific security pledged as collateral (at the ISIN level), the volume, maturity, repo rate, and
haircut. Coverage runs from January 2019 to June 2024 and spans both the June 2021 in-
troduction of the binding leverage-ratio requirement and multiple ECB rate-change events.
Crucially, transactions can be linked to dealer- and collateral-level characteristics, allowing us
to bring the three frictions we study together in a single empirical framework. 3 Consistent
with existing evidence (Hempel et al., 2023; Bejarano et al., 2025; Julliard et al., 2026; Her-
mes et al., 2025b; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), the data confirm that trade-level haircuts
in the bilateral segment are frequently zero, occasionally carry the “wrong” sign relative to
2Repo contracts embed additional risk management tools beyond the initial haircut, most notably daily
margining. Margining refers to the daily mark-to-market adjustment of the collateral value, which requires the
posting of variation margin when price changes alter the exposure between counterparties. While the haircut pro-
vides an ex ante buffer against potential losses in the event of default, daily margining manages ex post exposure
by ensuring that the collateral value remains aligned with the outstanding cash position over the life of the trans-
action. Thus, although both mechanisms mitigate counterparty and market risk, they address distinct dimensions
of risk: haircuts protect against liquidation and replacement risk, whereas margining limits the accumulation of
mark-to-market losses.
3Dealer leverage ratios are sourced from the ECB’s harmonised financial reporting FINREP dataset.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
4

the direction of the trade, and depart from a monotonic dependence on collateral risk. For
example, there are periods in which haircuts on collateral from less risky countries are higher
than those on collateral from riskier countries. In short, we observe that many repo contracts
are priced as if there is no liquidation or replacement risk, and are even priced contrary to ex
ante expectations.
To rationalise these patterns and derive testable predictions, we develop a bilateral bar-
gaining model of the dealer-to-client repo market. Dealer and client jointly negotiate the
contract(r , h) through Nash bargaining in the spirit of Infante (2019). The model applies
to both collateral-driven and funding-driven segments, and embeds three frictions known to
shape repo markets in a single framework: dealer balance-sheet constraints (e.g., Ranaldo,
Schaffner, and Vasios, 2021), collateral convenience yields (e.g., Buraschi and Menini, 2002;
Corradin and Maddaloni, 2020; Arrata, Nguyen, Rahmouni-Rousseau, and Vari, 2020; Bal-
lensiefen, Ranaldo, and Winterberg, 2023), and client outside options (e.g., Eisenschmidt,
Ma, and Zhang, 2024). The model recovers the textbook risk-management haircuts when
the frictions vanish and delivers sharp segment-specific sign predictions: leverage constraints
raise haircuts in collateral-driven repos only, convenience yields flip sign across the two seg-
ments through a rehypothecation channel, and client outside options do the same through
the shadow value of the conserved resource (cash in collateral-driven trades, collateral in
funding-driven trades). Within this framework, zero and wrong-sign haircuts are equilibrium
contracting outcomes under regulatory and intermediation frictions, not departures from ra-
tional risk management.
We test these predictions in the MMSR data. First, we show that dealer balance-sheet con-
straints put upward pressure on haircuts in collateral-driven repos. From a dealer’s perspec-
tive, the regulatory treatment of repos and reverse repos is asymmetric: in collateral-driven
repos, the cash leg increases total assets and enters the non-risk-weighted leverage ratio,
making these trades balance-sheet intensive, whereas funding-driven repos do not tighten
the leverage constraint in the same way. 4 Moreover, haircuts also carry capital cost. Lower
haircuts in collateral-driven repos increase the amount of cash received by the dealer and
4This is because, under standard accounting treatments, securities received as collateral remain on the balance
sheet of the collateral provider, whereas the cash leg of the transaction is recognized as an asset on the bank’s
balance sheet.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
5

thus the balance-sheet usage, giving capital-constrained dealers an incentive to raise haircuts.
Consistent with this mechanism, we find, in thecross-section, that dealers with lower lever-
age ratios increased haircuts compared to less-constrained dealers after the introduction of
the binding leverage ratio requirements in 2021. Interestingly, dealers in German collateral
are — on average — more balance-sheet constrained than dealers in Italian securities, which
provides an intuition for why haircuts on collateral countries with higher convenience yields
and replacement risk can still be higher. In the time-series, we show that this effect has only
emerged since the leverage ratio requirements for dealer banks in the euro area have become
binding. Importantly, the leverage ratio in the euro area becomes binding only on reporting
days (quarter-end days), however, euro area banks are also required to report an “averaging”
version of their leverage ratio. In line with this, we show that the effect of the leverage ratio
on haircuts is present not only on quarter-end days but throughout the entire quarter. As the
leverage ratio regulation does not penalize reverse repos, there is no effect on funding-driven
repos.
We document these empirical patterns both at the transaction level and at the dealer–
client–day level. This dual approach mitigates concerns that haircuts are determined at the
client portfolio level rather than at the level of individual transactions. Consistent with this
interpretation, we show that the distribution of transaction-level haircuts closely mirrors the
distribution implied by dealer–client–day aggregated cash and collateral positions. The tight
correspondence between these measures suggests that our haircut estimates are not mate-
rially distorted by portfolio-level margining practices and is consistent with institutional
features documented for the U.S. Treasury repo market (Hempel et al., 2023). 5 Figure 1
illustrates these results: after the introduction of the leverage ratio requirement, the most
leverage-constrained dealers increased haircuts relative to less-constrained dealers, but only
in collateral-driven trades.
Second, we show that the same collateral characteristic can push haircuts in opposite
directions across collateral- and funding-driven trades. In collateral-driven trades, the dealer
lends the bond to the client and bears the replacement risk of not receiving it back at maturity.
5For example, Hempel et al. (2023) highlight that in bilateral repo transactions transaction-level haircuts
determine margins collected for that transaction, whereas for centrally cleared repos, margins are calculated on
the portfolio level.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
6

Bonds with higher convenience yields are scarcer and more valuable to market participants
(Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012; Ballensiefen and Ranaldo, 2023), which makes
them costlier to re-source in the case of counterparty default. Higher convenience yields
therefore push haircuts down in the collateral-driven segment, as dealers demand more cash
upfront to insure against this replacement cost. In funding-driven trades, by contrast, the
dealer receives the bond from the client and holds it for the term of the repo. Because the
dealer can rehypothecate the bond during that time, receiving a scarcer or more valuable bond
is more profitable. Higher convenience yields therefore raise haircuts in the funding-driven
segment: dealers require the client to post more collateral per unit of cash lent, allowing them
to accumulate more of the valuable bond. This sign flip reflects the fundamentally different
economic role of the haircut in each segment.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
7

Third, we show that client outside options push haircuts in opposite directions across
the two segments. In funding-driven trades, the client borrows cash from the dealer and
posts collateral. The client prefers a lower haircut, as this means posting less collateral per
unit of cash borrowed. Consistent with this, clients with a broader network of active dealer
relationships negotiate systematically lower haircuts. In collateral-driven trades, by contrast,
the client lends cash to the dealer and receives a specific security. The client prefers a higher
haircut, as this means receiving more collateral per unit of cash lent. Consistent with this,
clients with broader outside options negotiate systematically higher (less negative) haircuts.
The same underlying client characteristic therefore pushes haircuts in opposite directions
across the two segments. Overall, this result implies that haircut levels are relationship-
specific and shaped by client outside options, rather than adjusting only to time-varying
collateral risk.
Building on these frictions, the model yields two testable predictions for repo rates in the
collateral-driven segment: (i) constrained dealers exhibit higher repo-rate volatility, and (ii)
they transmit ECB deposit-facility-rate changes less completely to their clients. We confirm
both in the data. Funding-driven trades, in which dealer leverage constraints have no effect on
the haircut, serve as natural placebos: rate volatility and pass-through in the funding-driven
segment are unrelated to dealer leverage. These results suggest that post-crisis leverage-
ratio regulation carries unintended consequences for monetary policy transmission, operating
through the composition of the repo contract.
In sum, we provide evidence that haircuts in repo markets are shaped by different fric-
tions across collateral- and funding-driven segments. The remainder of the paper proceeds as
follows. After introducing the related literature, Section 2 describes the institutional setting.
Section 3 develops the bargaining model and derives its haircut and rate predictions. Sec-
tion 4 introduces our data, Section 5 tests the model’s haircut predictions on transaction-level
data, documenting how the three frictions shape haircut design in the collateral-driven and
funding-driven segments. Section 6 tests the model’s rate-level predictions on volatility and
monetary policy pass-through. Section 7 concludes.
Related literature. Our analysis mainly contributes to two strands of the literature. First,
we add to work on haircut determination in bilateral repo markets. Dang, Gorton, and Holm-
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
8

ström (2011) argue theoretically that haircuts exist to make collateralised debt “information-
insensitive.” A growing empirical literature, however, documents that trade-level haircuts
in bilateral repo are systematically zero or negative across jurisdictions — Europe (Hermes
et al., 2025a,b; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), the United States (Hempel et al., 2023; Bejarano
et al., 2025; Kahn and McCormick, 2025; Cenicola et al., 2025), and the United Kingdom
(Julliard et al., 2026). Recent contributions have advanced several explanations: competition
among lenders (Bittner and Jank, 2025), excess balance-sheet capacity (Bejarano et al., 2025),
portfolio-level margining that substitutes for trade-level haircuts (Hempel et al., 2023; Hill
and Westphal, 2025; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), wrong-way-risk premia between bor-
rower and collateral (Barbiero, Schepens, and Sigaux, 2024), and dealer market power over
less-connected clients (Hau, Hoffmann, Langfield, and Timmer, 2021).
We contribute several distinct channels in explaining these repo haircut patterns by sys-
tematically distinguishing betweencollateral- and funding-driven repo transactions: the Basel III
leverage ratio as a first-order regulatory friction shaping haircut design in the collateral-driven
segment of the euro-area bilateral repo market. We further document the first systematic evi-
dence of segment-level asymmetry: convenience yields and client outside options act in oppo-
site directions across collateral- and funding-driven repos. These channels operate alongside,
and are distinct from, the portfolio-margining channel documented by Panzarino and Spo-
laore (2026) and the wrong-way-risk channel of Barbiero et al. (2024). Whereas Bejarano
et al. (2025) document how the zero risk-weight of Treasury repo enables U.S. dealers to sup-
ply leverage to non-bank clients through negative haircuts, we identify the opposite margin
— the leverage ratio constrains euro-area dealers and pushes haircuts upward in collateral-
driven trades. The paper also relates to work on collateral demand and specialness in repo
markets (e.g., Mancini, Ranaldo, and Wrampelmeyer, 2016; Arrata et al., 2020; Corradin and
Maddaloni, 2020; Coen, Coen, and Hüser, 2024).6
Second, we add to the literature on monetary policy, financial regulation, and the trans-
mission process (e.g., Duffie and Krishnamurthy, 2016; Drechsler, Savov, and Schnabl, 2017;
Ballensiefen et al., 2023; Eisenschmidt et al., 2024). Post-crisis bank regulation has been shown
6Studies on safe-asset scarcity show that high-quality government bonds in Europe command convenience
yields that translate into repo pricing (Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012; Ballensiefen and Ranaldo,
2023). Gorton and Metrick (2012) document how repo haircuts spiked during the 2008 financial crisis.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
9

to distort short-term funding markets: Ranaldo et al. (2021) document quarter-end window
dressing by European banks around the Basel III leverage ratio, Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan
(2018) document persistent covered-interest-parity deviations attributable to bank balance-
sheet constraints, and Eisenschmidt et al. (2024) show that dealer market power in OTC repo
reduces policy-rate pass-through. We advance this literature on two dimensions. First, we
show that the leverage ratio reshapes euro-area repo not only at quarter-ends but throughout
the entire quarter, and that it operates through haircut design rather than only through rates.
Second, we identify a distinct within-dealer-sector transmission channel: because constrained
dealers cannot use haircuts as an adjustment margin, the shock is displaced onto repo-rate
volatility and onto the pass-through of policy rates to non-bank clients. These findings res-
onate with Duffie and Krishnamurthy (2016) and Drechsler et al. (2017) on the imperfect
transmission of central-bank rates through frictions in intermediary balance sheets.
Lastly, we develop a theoretical model that rationalises our empirical findings. Our frame-
work is a bilateral Nash bargaining model in the spirit of Infante (2019), reflecting the OTC
search-and-bargaining structure of the dealer-to-client segment (Duffie, Gârleanu, and Peder-
sen, 2005). It jointly determines the equilibrium haircut and repo rate under dealer balance-
sheet costs, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options, and is augmented with
a framework-commitment refinement that delivers closed-form predictions for rate volatil-
ity and monetary-policy pass-through. This complements existing theoretical work on hair-
cuts as information-insensitive risk mitigants (Dang et al., 2011), on margin-driven ampli-
fication of financial cycles (Geanakoplos, 2010; Brunnermeier and Pedersen, 2009), and on
the intermediary-balance-sheet view of asset pricing (Adrian and Shin, 2010; He and Krish-
namurthy, 2013), by embedding a specific regulatory friction — the leverage ratio — as a
first-order determinant of equilibrium contract terms.
2. Institutional background
Repurchase agreement. A repurchase agreement, or repo, is a short-term secured financing
transaction in which one counterparty sells a security (most commonly a sovereign bond) to
another, with an obligation to repurchase it at a predetermined price after an agreed period.
A repo contract is characterised by four key terms, each negotiated at the transaction level:
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
10

(i) the volume of cash exchanged, (ii) the repo rate, (iii) the specific security posted as collat-
eral, and (iv) the haircut applied to the collateral. 7 The collateralised nature of repos means
they serve a dual function: they provide a vehicle both for obtaining short-term funding and
for sourcing specific securities.
Euro area repo market structure. The euro area repo market comprises two broad segments:
an inter-dealer segment, in which dealers trade with one another, and adealer-to-client segment,
in which dealers intermediate trades with non-dealer institutions such as investment funds,
hedge funds, money market funds, insurance companies, and pension funds. The inter-
dealer segment is predominantly centrally cleared. Transactions in the inter-dealer market are
executed on electronic platforms (such as BrokerTec, Eurex Repo, and MTS Repo) and novated
to a central counterparty (CCP), which becomes the legal counterparty to both sides of each
trade. Central clearing allows dealers to net their positions against a single counterparty
across many trades, substantially reducing gross balance-sheet exposures. Moreover, the
CCP applies standardised risk-management tools, including initial and variation margin, and
facilitates efficient price formation through anonymous order books. 8 The dealer-to-client
segment, by contrast, is an over-the-counter (OTC) bilateral market. Because netting is only
possible within each individual dealer–client relationship, gross exposures remain larger and
balance-sheet constraints are more binding than in centrally cleared markets. There is no
centralised price formation mechanism; instead, contract terms are negotiated bilaterally and
are relationship-specific.
The focus of this paper is on the bilateral dealer-to-client segment of the euro area money
market, which provides a uniquely suitable setting to study how repo haircuts are set in
collateral- and funding-driven environments. This segment is characterised by bilateral con-
tracting, relationship-specific bargaining, and limited transparency, making market frictions
particularly salient. Moreover, the dealer-to-client segment represents the primary channel
through which monetary policy is transmitted from regulated dealer banks to non-bank fi-
nancial institutions, allowing us to study directly how regulatory constraints affect both con-
7The cash lender in a repo transaction becomes the legal owner of the collateral for the term of the repo, and
may use it for example, to settle delivery obligations or to re-pledge in a subsequent transaction (Duffie, 1996).
8For cleared transactions, it is common practice to report a zero haircut because risk management is handled
through the CCP’s initial and variation margin framework. Our focus on the bilateral segment avoids this con-
found. See also Schaffner, Ranaldo, and Tsatsaronis (2019) for evidence on dealer trading patterns and home bias
in the inter-dealer segment.

11

tract design and policy pass-through. Overall, the bilateral dealer-to-client segment is a subset
of the broader bilateral repo market, which itself accounts for a substantial share of euro-area
repo activity (Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026).
Funding-driven versus collateral-driven repos. A key distinction for this paper is between
funding-driven and collateral-driven repo transactions. In a funding-driven repo, the initiating
party seeks cash; in a collateral-driven repo, the initiating party seeks a specific security or,
more broadly, eligible collateral. This distinction matters fundamentally for the economics
of haircut-setting. In a funding-driven repo, the haircut protects the cash lender against the
liquidation risk of the collateral in the event of borrower default. The cash lender, therefore,
has an incentive to demand overcollateralisation, implying positive haircuts. In a collateral-
driven repo, the haircut protects the collateral provider (the dealer) against the replacement
risk of the security: should the cash lender default and fail to return the collateral, the dealer
must repurchase it in the open market, potentially at a premium. The dealer, therefore, has
an incentive to deliver less cash than the collateral is worth, implying negative haircuts.
3. Theoretical Framework
We develop a bilateral bargaining model in which a dealer and a client jointly negotiate
the haircut and the repo rate, matching the institutional structure of the euro-area bilateral
dealer-to-client repo market segment. The model embeds three frictions in a single framework:
dealer balance-sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. It
applies to both the collateral-driven and funding-driven segments, recovers the textbook risk-
management haircuts when the three frictions vanish, and shows how each friction shifts
haircuts within each segment.
A dealer d and a client c negotiate the contract (r, h) over collateral issued by country j.
Let C and V denote the cash exchanged and the market value of the collateral at inception.

3.4. Comparative statics
The equilibrium haircuts are explicit ratios of the fundamentals, so differentiation gives
sign predictions for how each friction shifts the haircut in each segment. We state these as
three corollaries, one for each friction.
Corollary 1 (Balance-sheet constraints): The collateral-driven haircut increases with the dealer’s
balance-sheet cost, ∂h∗CD,j/∂Γj = (1 − h∗CD,j)/(Φ + Γj) > 0 whenever the cash leg is positive, while
the funding-driven haircut is unaffected, ∂h∗FD,j/∂Γj = 0. The asymmetry follows from the regulatory
treatment: only the cash leg 1 − h received in a collateral-driven trade expands the dealer’s non-
risk-weighted exposure measure. A constrained dealer, therefore, raises the collateral-driven haircut
to reduce her cash intake and free up balance-sheet capacity. She has no analogous margin in the
funding-driven segment, where the reverse-repo leg does not consume leverage-ratio capacity.

3.5. Framework commitment and residual rate adjustment
The equilibrium in Proposition 1 treats (h, r) as jointly renegotiated on each trade. In
practice, bilateral repo relationships are governed by master framework agreements, most
commonly the Global Master Repurchase Agreement (GMRA), which specify haircut sched-
ules at the dealer–client level and are refreshed at agreed intervals, typically quarterly. Each
schedule indexes haircuts by collateral characteristics (issuer country, rating, maturity, size),
and every trade evaluates the schedule at its own coordinates. Between refresh dates, the hair-
cut at any given schedule row is effectively committed; only the rate is renegotiated on each
trade. This institutional feature is compatible with our empirical strategy: the transaction-
level heterogeneity we exploit reflects variation across schedule rows (different collateral)
and across dealer–client pairs (different schedules), not trade-level renegotiation of a fixed
schedule entry.
We accommodate this feature with a two-stage refinement that preserves the comparative
statics on h from Corollaries 1–3 and adds closed-form predictions for the rate. At Stage 0, the
dealer–client pair Nash-bargains over h given expected fundamentals ( ¯Γj, ¯yj, ¯λ, ¯λc). Because
payoffs remain quasi-linear in r, the transferable-utility separation applies unchanged, and
the commitment haircut is the tangency solution of Proposition 1 evaluated at expectations,

4. Data
This section describes the data used in our analysis.
4.1. Data
MMSR.Our primary data source is the Money Market Statistical Reporting (MMSR) dataset,
a confidential supervisory dataset collected by the European Central Bank. The MMSR re-
quires 53 euro area banks to report daily transaction-level information on all their euro-
denominated money market activity, covering both secured (repo) and unsecured segments.10
The secured segment covers all repo transactions with a maturity of up to one year.11 For each
transaction, we observe the repo rate, the volume, the maturity, the haircut, the collateral se-
curity at the ISIN level, and identifiers for both the reporting dealer and the counterparty,
including the counterparty’s sector classification. Our sample covers the period from January
2019 to June 2024. 12
SFTDS.We cross-check our results using the Securities Financing Transaction Data Store
(SFTDS) dataset used, for instance, by Hermes et al. (2025b). SFTDS data only start in 2021.
Due to the longer time frame, we, therefore, focus on the MMSR sample for the main part of
our analysis. As we show in the paper, SFTR-based evidence on bilateral margin levels and
counterparty composition (Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026) is directionally consistent with our
haircut evidence, supporting external validity.
Sample restrictions. We impose several restrictions to obtain a sample that is well suited to
studying haircut determination in the bilateral dealer-to-client segment. First, we restrict the
sample to bilateral (non-CCP-cleared) repo transactions in which the reporting agent is the
dealer and the counterparty is a non-dealer client. This excludes inter-dealer trades and CCP-
cleared transactions, where haircuts follow standardised schedules and margining is handled
by the clearing house rather than negotiated bilaterally. Second, we focus on transactions

5. Empirical Analysis
In our analysis, we consider three main money-market frictions and their impact on repo hair-
cuts: (i) dealer balance-sheet constraints, (ii) the convenience yield embedded in the collateral
value, and (iii) client outside options.
5.1. Dealer balance sheet constraints
The post-crisis leverage ratio (LR) regulation treats repo transactions asymmetrically. Lending
collateral against cash in a collateral-driven repo extends the dealer’s balance sheet, whereas
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
30

lending cash against collateral in a funding-driven reverse repo does not. Because the cash
received in a collateral-driven trade increases one-for-one with a more negative haircut, con-
strained dealers can free leverage capacity by raising haircuts in the collateral-driven segment.
Ranaldo et al. (2021) document a related asymmetry for repo rates around quarter-ends; we
show that the same asymmetry operates on the haircut margin, and that it is present through-
out the entire quarter rather than only at reporting dates.
On June 28, 2021, the 3% LR requirement under the EU’s Capital Requirements Regulation
II (CRR II) became a binding Pillar 1 obligation for all ECB-supervised banks. Article 429e
permits netting of securities financing transactions only under narrow conditions, notably
identical counterparties and settlement dates. Matched-book intermediation across different
clients, therefore, expands gross exposure on both legs and directly consumes scarce leverage
capacity. The effective date of the implementation was predetermined years in advance, the
timing of the shock was, therefore, exogenous to contemporaneous conditions in the repo
market. Cross-sectional dispersion in how close each dealer sits to the 3% threshold generates
variation in treatment intensity.
Euro-area banks must report both a point-in-time and an averaged version of the lever-
age ratio, we, therefore, expect dealer banks to internalise the constraint in their day-to-day
haircut setting throughout the quarter, not only around reporting dates. Cross-sectional dif-
ferences in dealer balance-sheet capacity should, therefore, shape haircuts throughout the
entire quarter. To test this, we sort dealers each quarter into LR terciles and estimate the
following transaction-level difference-in-difference estimation:

Haircuts are only one of many margins through which dealers manage the leverage-ratio
constraint. Two features of our estimates nevertheless make the haircut adjustment econom-

appearing asymmetrically across collateral- and funding-driven trades, monotonically in the
cross-section of dealer headroom, and persistently both at reporting dates and throughout the
quarter. Together, these patterns indicate that the leverage-ratio shadow cost is internalised
at the transaction margin, creating an incentive for constrained dealers to hand out zero or
even positive haircuts in collateral-driven trades rather than the negative haircuts that would
optimally hedge replacement risk. As we show in Section 6, the economic consequence of
this distortion is the resulting spillover onto repo-rate volatility and the transmission of ECB
policy rates to non-bank clients.

rather than individually for each transaction. If a dealer and client agree on a standing haircut

and statistically significant across all collateral-driven specifications, and, if anything, some-

again shows no effect, indicating that the pricing pattern is specific to the segment in which
the leverage ratio binds.

5.2. Convenience yields
Having examined how dealer balance-sheet constraints shape haircuts, we now turn to the
role of collateral characteristics. Assets used as collateral in bilateral repo differ substantially
in their scarcity, specialness, and value to market participants. Because these characteristics
affect the dealer’s risk exposure differently across collateral- and funding-driven trades, they
should transmit into haircut design asymmetrically across the two segments. In the preceding
analysis we examined how dealer’s balance-sheet constraints shape haircuts. Of course, client
and collateral characteristics should also matter. A large literature documents that investors
pay a convenience premium for the safety and liquidity services embedded in high-quality
assets (Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012; Gorton, 2017), and that this premium
is reflected in repo rates (Duffie and Krishnamurthy, 2016; Ballensiefen and Ranaldo, 2023).
Convenience yields vary across securities (driven by differences in issuer credit quality, re-
ECB Working Paper Series No 3301
35

maining maturity, and benchmark status) and over time with the opportunity cost of holding
money (Nagel, 2016) or macroeconomic uncertainty (Moreira and Savov, 2017). Yet, while the
link between convenience yields and repo rates is well established, far less is known about
how convenience yields affect the haircut margin.
We argue that convenience yields should influence haircuts in opposite directions across
the two segments. In a collateral-driven repo, the dealer pledges a specific bond in exchange
for cash; if the counterparty defaults and fails to return the security, the dealer must repur-
chase a potentially scarce asset in the open market. The higher the convenience yield on the
pledged bond, the costlier this replacement and the greater the dealer’s incentive to protect
herself by demanding a lower haircut, i.e., demanding more cash in return for the collateral
pledged. In a funding-driven repo, the dealer receives the bond from the client in exchange
for cash and holds it during the term of the trade. As legal owner, she can re-use the collateral
by pledging it in another repo, delivering it against a short, or posting it as regulatory margin,
and thereby captures a fraction of its convenience yield through rehypothecation. This makes
higher-convenience-yield collateral more valuable to hold, giving the dealer an incentive to
demand more of it per euro of cash lent, i.e., a higher haircut. A standard liquidation-risk
channel, in which more liquid collateral is easier to sell at a smaller discount upon default,
would push in the opposite direction, but we argue that the rehypothecation channel dom-
inates in bilateral repo. Under this framework, we expect the convenience-yield effect to be
negative in the collateral-driven segment through replacement-risk protection, and positive
in the funding-driven segment through the rehypothecation channel.

Overall, the results are in line with Corollary 2. More precisely, in the collateral-driven
segment, across all four specifications, the convenience yield enters with a negative and sta-
tistically significant coefficient. For example, the point estimate in specification 3 implies
that a 100 basis-point increase in the ISIN-level convenience yield reduces haircuts by ap-
proximately 14 basis points. This is consistent with the replacement-risk channel: when the
pledged bond carries a high convenience premium, the dealer demands more cash in return
for parting with it, reflected in a lower haircut, so as to be better insured against the cost of
replacing a scarce and valuable security in the event of counterparty default.
In the funding-driven sample (Columns 5–8), by contrast, the convenience yield enters
with a positive and highly significant coefficient. This sign flip contradicts the risk-management
prior: safer, more valuable collateral should require less over-collateralisation, not more. The
result points instead to a different economic channel: rehypothecation. Because the dealer be-
comes the legal owner of the received bond for the term of the repo, they can rehypothecate it
in ways that scale with its specialness: re-pledging it in a subsequent collateral-driven trade at
the specialness premium, delivering it against a short position, or lending it in the securities-
lending market. The higher the convenience yield on the received bond, the more profitable
these re-use opportunities and the greater the dealer’s incentive to accumulate more collateral
per euro of cash lent, which translates into a higher haircut. Our results seem to suggest that,
in the funding-driven segment, the rehypothecation channel dominates the risk-management
channel.
5.3. Client outside options
A third key friction in the bilateral money market arises from market power. Establishing
and maintaining trading relationships in OTC markets is costly and time-consuming, limiting
the number of dealer links that clients can form. As a result, dealer banks may exercise mar-
ket power over their OTC counterparties (Eisenschmidt et al., 2024; Bittner and Jank, 2025).
To analyze the impact of dealer market power on repo haircuts, we estimate transaction-

fragmentos_texto.texto: Working Paper Series Stop believing in haircuts - at least the way you think about them Benedikt Ballensiefen, Jasper Knyphausen, Benoît Nguyen Disclaimer: This paper should not be reported as representing the views of the European Central Bank (ECB). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the ECB. No 3301 / October 2026

Abstract We study how frictions impact haircut setting in repo markets. Using transaction-level super- visory data and exploiting the 2021 introduction of the binding leverage ratio requirement, we show that three frictions jointly shape haircuts in the bilateral dealer-to-client segment: dealer balance sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. In collateral-driven repos, binding leverage constraints and broader client outside options both raise haircuts, while higher convenience yields push them down. In funding-driven trades, the leverage constraint has no effect, higher convenience yields raise haircuts through the rehypothecation channel, and broader client outside options lower them. We rationalise these patterns in a bilateral bargaining model with periodic haircut renegotiation. Consistent with the model, constrained dealers exhibit higher repo-rate volatility and weaker pass-through of ECB policy rate changes in the collateral-driven segment. Post-crisis bank regulation thus carries potential unintended consequences for repo market functioning and the transmission of monetary policy. J.E.L. classification: C78, E43, E52, E58, G12, G21, G28. Keywords: Bilateral repo, haircuts, dealer balance sheet, convenience yield, client outside options, leverage ratio, monetary policy pass-through. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 1

Non-technical Summary Repo is the largest segment of money markets: cash is borrowed against securities pledged as collateral, most often government bonds. Market participants use repo either to obtain cash (funding-driven repos) or to borrow specific securities (collateral-driven repos). In both cases, the haircut — the difference between the value of the collateral and the cash exchanged — is commonly viewed as a risk-management tool. It should be positive when a dealer lends cash, protecting it against having to sell the collateral at a loss if the client defaults, and negative when a dealer lends a security, protecting it against having to buy the security back at a higher price if it is not returned. In practice, haircuts in bilateral repo are mostly zero and often carry the opposite sign. This paper asks what explains these patterns. Using transaction-level data on euro area bilateral dealer-to-client repos from 2019 to 2024, we show that haircuts are shaped by three frictions. First, dealer balance-sheet constraints matter. The Basel III leverage ratio makes it costly for dealers to receive cash in collateral- driven repos, so dealers closer to their regulatory minimum set higher haircuts in these trades. This effect emerges once the leverage ratio becomes binding in June 2021, is present through- out the quarter rather than only at reporting dates, and is absent in funding-driven repos, which do not expand the dealer’s balance sheet in the same way. Second, the convenience yield of the collateral matters. Scarce, highly valued government bonds lower haircuts in collateral-driven trades, where dealers seek protection against the cost of replacing them, but raise haircuts in funding-driven trades, where dealers can re-use the bonds they receive. Third, clients’ outside options matter as clients with more dealer relationships obtain more favourable haircut terms. A bargaining model between dealer and

client rationalises these findings. It recovers the textbook risk-management haircuts when the frictions are absent and shows that zero and opposite-sign haircuts are equilibrium outcomes once regulation, collateral scarcity and client bargaining positions are taken into account. Consistent with the model, leverage-constrained dealers exhibit more volatile repo rates and pass changes in the ECB’s deposit facility rate through to their clients less completely in collateral-driven trades. Post-crisis bank regulation therefore has consequences not only for repo contract terms but also for the transmission of monetary policy in the repo market. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 2

1. Introduction Repurchase agreements (repo) — short-term loans secured by securities pledged as collat- eral, most often government bonds — are the main segment of the money market and play a central role in the efficient allocation of short-term funding, securities financing, and circula- tion of collateral. A deep and well-functioning repo market allows financial intermediaries to manage liquidity, enables non-bank financial institutions to finance leveraged portfolios, and as the largest segment of the money market is an essential step to transmit monetary policy to the broader financial system. Given its importance for market efficiency, financial stability, and the real economy, understanding the frictions that arise in the repo market — and the mechanisms through which they shape market outcomes — is essential. Haircuts applied to the collateral leg of repo transactions are generally assumed to be a key risk-management tool. Yet a growing body of evidence documents that haircuts in bilateral repo are systematically at zero or even negative across major jurisdictions — Europe (Hermes, Schmeling, and Schrimpf, 2025a,b; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), the United States (Hempel, Kahn, Mann, and Paddrik, 2023; Bejarano, Lu, and Wallen, 2025; Kahn and McCormick, 2025; Cenicola, Mann, and Paddrik, 2025), and the United Kingdom (Julliard, Pinter, Todorov, and Yuan, 2026). This pattern has revived the policy debate over the financial-stability risks posed by repo and the associated leverage of non-bank financial institutions, and has led the Fi- nancial Stability Board to propose, for instance, the imposition of minimum haircut floors (Financial Stability Board, 2025; Grill, Hermes, and Wedow, 2025). This paper identifies three money-market frictions — dealer balance-sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options — that jointly determine haircut design in bilateral repo markets, and analyses what these design choices imply for funding conditions, monetary policy transmis- sion, and financial stability.

In our analysis, we focus on the bilateral dealer-to-client segment of the repo market where haircuts are the result of a negotiation between the dealer bank and a client such as a hedge fund. 1 Repos serve a dual purpose in either providing cash or collateral. We 1By contrast, transactions in the inter-dealer segment tend to be centrally cleared with standardized haircuts. Because dealers have access to a centrally cleared interdealer market—offering capital netting benefits, anonymous centralized trading, homogeneous counterparty risk, and efficient price discovery—we assume that most trades in the dealer-to-client segment are client-initiated. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 3

classify transactions in which a dealer provides cash to a client as funding-driven and those in which a dealer provides collateral as collateral-driven. The haircut is defined as the percentage difference between the market value of the collateral pledged and the cash lent. The basic intuition behind collateralised lending is that haircuts should protect the cash- or collateral- lender from the counterparty’s default, and that rates are a function of supply and demand for cash and scarce collateral. If a dealer lends out cash (in a funding-driven transaction), we would expect haircuts to be positive to protect the dealer against a borrower default; if the borrower defaults, the dealer must sell the collateral at a potentially lower price than at inception. We refer to this risk as liquidation risk. By contrast, if a dealer lends out collateral (in a collateral-driven transaction), we would expect haircuts to be negative to protect dealers against the risk of the collateral not being returned. If the collateral is not returned, the dealer must re-source it in the market at a potentially higher price. We refer to this risk asreplacement risk.2 For our empirical analysis, we exploit the ECB’s Money Market Statistical Reporting (MMSR), a confidential supervisory database of the transaction-level activity of the largest dealer banks in the euro-area money market. MMSR offers an exceptionally rich window into the bilateral repo market: for each transaction we observe both counterparties, the spe- cific security pledged as collateral (at the ISIN level), the volume, maturity, repo rate, and haircut. Coverage runs from January 2019 to June 2024 and spans both the June 2021 in- troduction of the binding leverage-ratio requirement and multiple ECB rate-change events. Crucially, transactions can be linked to dealer- and collateral-level characteristics, allowing us to bring the three frictions we study together in

a single empirical framework. 3 Consistent with existing evidence (Hempel et al., 2023; Bejarano et al., 2025; Julliard et al., 2026; Her- mes et al., 2025b; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), the data confirm that trade-level haircuts in the bilateral segment are frequently zero, occasionally carry the “wrong” sign relative to 2Repo contracts embed additional risk management tools beyond the initial haircut, most notably daily margining. Margining refers to the daily mark-to-market adjustment of the collateral value, which requires the posting of variation margin when price changes alter the exposure between counterparties. While the haircut pro- vides an ex ante buffer against potential losses in the event of default, daily margining manages ex post exposure by ensuring that the collateral value remains aligned with the outstanding cash position over the life of the trans- action. Thus, although both mechanisms mitigate counterparty and market risk, they address distinct dimensions of risk: haircuts protect against liquidation and replacement risk, whereas margining limits the accumulation of mark-to-market losses. 3Dealer leverage ratios are sourced from the ECB’s harmonised financial reporting FINREP dataset. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 4

the direction of the trade, and depart from a monotonic dependence on collateral risk. For example, there are periods in which haircuts on collateral from less risky countries are higher than those on collateral from riskier countries. In short, we observe that many repo contracts are priced as if there is no liquidation or replacement risk, and are even priced contrary to ex ante expectations. To rationalise these patterns and derive testable predictions, we develop a bilateral bar- gaining model of the dealer-to-client repo market. Dealer and client jointly negotiate the contract(r , h) through Nash bargaining in the spirit of Infante (2019). The model applies to both collateral-driven and funding-driven segments, and embeds three frictions known to shape repo markets in a single framework: dealer balance-sheet constraints (e.g., Ranaldo, Schaffner, and Vasios, 2021), collateral convenience yields (e.g., Buraschi and Menini, 2002; Corradin and Maddaloni, 2020; Arrata, Nguyen, Rahmouni-Rousseau, and Vari, 2020; Bal- lensiefen, Ranaldo, and Winterberg, 2023), and client outside options (e.g., Eisenschmidt, Ma, and Zhang, 2024). The model recovers the textbook risk-management haircuts when the frictions vanish and delivers sharp segment-specific sign predictions: leverage constraints raise haircuts in collateral-driven repos only, convenience yields flip sign across the two seg- ments through a rehypothecation channel, and client outside options do the same through the shadow value of the conserved resource (cash in collateral-driven trades, collateral in funding-driven trades). Within this framework, zero and wrong-sign haircuts are equilibrium contracting outcomes under regulatory and intermediation frictions, not departures from ra- tional risk management. We test these predictions in the MMSR data. First, we show that dealer balance-sheet con- straints put upward pressure on haircuts in collateral-driven repos. From a dealer’s perspec- tive, the regulatory treatment of repos and reverse repos is asymmetric: in collateral-driven repos, the cash leg increases total assets

and enters the non-risk-weighted leverage ratio, making these trades balance-sheet intensive, whereas funding-driven repos do not tighten the leverage constraint in the same way. 4 Moreover, haircuts also carry capital cost. Lower haircuts in collateral-driven repos increase the amount of cash received by the dealer and 4This is because, under standard accounting treatments, securities received as collateral remain on the balance sheet of the collateral provider, whereas the cash leg of the transaction is recognized as an asset on the bank’s balance sheet. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 5

thus the balance-sheet usage, giving capital-constrained dealers an incentive to raise haircuts. Consistent with this mechanism, we find, in thecross-section, that dealers with lower lever- age ratios increased haircuts compared to less-constrained dealers after the introduction of the binding leverage ratio requirements in 2021. Interestingly, dealers in German collateral are — on average — more balance-sheet constrained than dealers in Italian securities, which provides an intuition for why haircuts on collateral countries with higher convenience yields and replacement risk can still be higher. In the time-series, we show that this effect has only emerged since the leverage ratio requirements for dealer banks in the euro area have become binding. Importantly, the leverage ratio in the euro area becomes binding only on reporting days (quarter-end days), however, euro area banks are also required to report an “averaging” version of their leverage ratio. In line with this, we show that the effect of the leverage ratio on haircuts is present not only on quarter-end days but throughout the entire quarter. As the leverage ratio regulation does not penalize reverse repos, there is no effect on funding-driven repos. We document these empirical patterns both at the transaction level and at the dealer– client–day level. This dual approach mitigates concerns that haircuts are determined at the client portfolio level rather than at the level of individual transactions. Consistent with this interpretation, we show that the distribution of transaction-level haircuts closely mirrors the distribution implied by dealer–client–day aggregated cash and collateral positions. The tight correspondence between these measures suggests that our haircut estimates are not mate- rially distorted by portfolio-level margining practices and is consistent with institutional features documented for the U.S. Treasury repo market (Hempel et al., 2023). 5 Figure 1 illustrates these results: after the introduction of the leverage ratio requirement, the most

leverage-constrained dealers increased haircuts relative to less-constrained dealers, but only in collateral-driven trades. Second, we show that the same collateral characteristic can push haircuts in opposite directions across collateral- and funding-driven trades. In collateral-driven trades, the dealer lends the bond to the client and bears the replacement risk of not receiving it back at maturity. 5For example, Hempel et al. (2023) highlight that in bilateral repo transactions transaction-level haircuts determine margins collected for that transaction, whereas for centrally cleared repos, margins are calculated on the portfolio level. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 6

Bonds with higher convenience yields are scarcer and more valuable to market participants (Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012; Ballensiefen and Ranaldo, 2023), which makes them costlier to re-source in the case of counterparty default. Higher convenience yields therefore push haircuts down in the collateral-driven segment, as dealers demand more cash upfront to insure against this replacement cost. In funding-driven trades, by contrast, the dealer receives the bond from the client and holds it for the term of the repo. Because the dealer can rehypothecate the bond during that time, receiving a scarcer or more valuable bond is more profitable. Higher convenience yields therefore raise haircuts in the funding-driven segment: dealers require the client to post more collateral per unit of cash lent, allowing them to
accumulate more of the valuable bond. This sign flip reflects the fundamentally different economic role of the haircut in each segment. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 7

Third, we show that client outside options push haircuts in opposite directions across the two segments. In funding-driven trades, the client borrows cash from the dealer and posts collateral. The client prefers a lower haircut, as this means posting less collateral per unit of cash borrowed. Consistent with this, clients with a broader network of active dealer relationships negotiate systematically lower haircuts. In collateral-driven trades, by contrast, the client lends cash to the dealer and receives a specific security. The client prefers a higher haircut, as this means receiving more collateral per unit of cash lent. Consistent with this, clients with broader outside options negotiate systematically higher (less negative) haircuts. The same underlying client characteristic therefore pushes haircuts in opposite directions across the two segments. Overall, this result implies that haircut levels are relationship- specific and shaped by client outside options, rather than adjusting only to time-varying collateral risk. Building on these frictions, the model yields two testable predictions for repo rates in the collateral-driven segment: (i) constrained dealers exhibit higher repo-rate volatility, and (ii) they transmit ECB deposit-facility-rate changes less completely to their clients. We confirm both in the data. Funding-driven trades, in which dealer leverage constraints have no effect on the haircut, serve as natural placebos: rate volatility and pass-through in the funding-driven segment are unrelated to dealer leverage. These results suggest that post-crisis leverage- ratio regulation carries unintended consequences for monetary policy transmission, operating through the composition of the repo contract. In sum, we provide evidence that haircuts in repo markets are shaped by different fric- tions across collateral- and funding-driven segments. The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. After introducing the related literature, Section 2 describes the institutional setting. Section 3 develops the bargaining model and derives its haircut and rate predictions. Sec- tion 4

introduces our data, Section 5 tests the model’s haircut predictions on transaction-level data, documenting how the three frictions shape haircut design in the collateral-driven and funding-driven segments. Section 6 tests the model’s rate-level predictions on volatility and monetary policy pass-through. Section 7 concludes. Related literature. Our analysis mainly contributes to two strands of the literature. First, we add to work on haircut determination in bilateral repo markets. Dang, Gorton, and Holm- ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 8

ström (2011) argue theoretically that haircuts exist to make collateralised debt “information- insensitive.” A growing empirical literature, however, documents that trade-level haircuts in bilateral repo are systematically zero or negative across jurisdictions — Europe (Hermes et al., 2025a,b; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), the United States (Hempel et al., 2023; Bejarano et al., 2025; Kahn and McCormick, 2025; Cenicola et al., 2025), and the United Kingdom (Julliard et al., 2026). Recent contributions have advanced several explanations: competition among lenders (Bittner and Jank, 2025), excess balance-sheet capacity (Bejarano et al., 2025), portfolio-level margining that substitutes for trade-level haircuts (Hempel et al., 2023; Hill and Westphal, 2025; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), wrong-way-risk premia between bor- rower and collateral (Barbiero, Schepens, and Sigaux, 2024), and dealer market power over less-connected clients (Hau, Hoffmann, Langfield, and Timmer, 2021). We contribute several distinct channels in explaining these repo haircut patterns by sys- tematically distinguishing betweencollateral- and funding-driven repo transactions: the Basel III leverage ratio as a first-order regulatory friction shaping haircut design in the collateral-driven segment of the euro-area bilateral repo market. We further document the first systematic evi- dence of segment-level asymmetry: convenience yields and client outside options act in oppo- site directions across collateral- and funding-driven repos. These channels operate alongside, and are distinct from, the portfolio-margining channel documented by Panzarino and Spo- laore (2026) and the wrong-way-risk channel of Barbiero et al. (2024). Whereas Bejarano et al. (2025) document how the zero risk-weight of Treasury repo enables U.S. dealers to sup- ply leverage to non-bank clients through negative haircuts, we identify the opposite margin — the leverage ratio constrains euro-area dealers and pushes haircuts upward in collateral- driven trades. The paper also relates to work on collateral demand and specialness in repo markets (e.g., Mancini, Ranaldo, and Wrampelmeyer, 2016; Arrata et al., 2020;

Corradin and Maddaloni, 2020; Coen, Coen, and Hüser, 2024).6 Second, we add to the literature on monetary policy, financial regulation, and the trans- mission process (e.g., Duffie and Krishnamurthy, 2016; Drechsler, Savov, and Schnabl, 2017; Ballensiefen et al., 2023; Eisenschmidt et al., 2024). Post-crisis bank regulation has been shown 6Studies on safe-asset scarcity show that high-quality government bonds in Europe command convenience yields that translate into repo pricing (Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012; Ballensiefen and Ranaldo, 2023). Gorton and Metrick (2012) document how repo haircuts spiked during the 2008 financial crisis. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 9

to distort short-term funding markets: Ranaldo et al. (2021) document quarter-end window dressing by European banks around the Basel III leverage ratio, Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018) document persistent covered-interest-parity deviations attributable to bank balance- sheet constraints, and Eisenschmidt et al. (2024) show that dealer market power in OTC repo reduces policy-rate pass-through. We advance this literature on two dimensions. First, we show that the leverage ratio reshapes euro-area repo not only at quarter-ends but throughout the entire quarter, and that it operates through haircut design rather than only through rates. Second, we identify a distinct within-dealer-sector transmission channel: because constrained dealers cannot use haircuts as an adjustment margin, the shock is displaced onto repo-rate volatility and onto the pass-through of policy rates to non-bank clients. These findings res- onate with Duffie and Krishnamurthy (2016) and Drechsler et al. (2017) on the imperfect transmission of central-bank rates through frictions in intermediary balance sheets. Lastly, we develop a theoretical model that rationalises our empirical findings. Our frame- work is a bilateral Nash bargaining model in the spirit of Infante (2019), reflecting the OTC search-and-bargaining structure of the dealer-to-client segment (Duffie, Gârleanu, and Peder- sen, 2005). It jointly determines the equilibrium haircut and repo rate under dealer balance- sheet costs, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options, and is augmented with a framework-commitment refinement that delivers closed-form predictions for rate volatil- ity and monetary-policy pass-through. This complements existing theoretical work on hair- cuts as information-insensitive risk mitigants (Dang et al., 2011), on margin-driven ampli- fication of financial cycles (Geanakoplos, 2010; Brunnermeier and Pedersen, 2009), and on the intermediary-balance-sheet view of asset pricing (Adrian and Shin, 2010; He and Krish- namurthy, 2013), by embedding a specific regulatory friction — the leverage ratio — as a first-order determinant of equilibrium contract terms. 2. Institutional

background Repurchase agreement. A repurchase agreement, or repo, is a short-term secured financing transaction in which one counterparty sells a security (most commonly a sovereign bond) to another, with an obligation to repurchase it at a predetermined price after an agreed period. A repo contract is characterised by four key terms, each negotiated at the transaction level: ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 10

(i) the volume of cash exchanged, (ii) the repo rate, (iii) the specific security posted as collat- eral, and (iv) the haircut applied to the collateral. 7 The collateralised nature of repos means they serve a dual function: they provide a vehicle both for obtaining short-term funding and for sourcing specific securities. Euro area repo market structure. The euro area repo market comprises two broad segments: an inter-dealer segment, in which dealers trade with one another, and adealer-to-client segment, in which dealers intermediate trades with non-dealer institutions such as investment funds, hedge funds, money market funds, insurance companies, and pension funds. The inter- dealer segment is predominantly centrally cleared. Transactions in the inter-dealer market are executed on electronic platforms (such as BrokerTec, Eurex Repo, and MTS Repo) and novated to a central counterparty (CCP), which becomes the legal counterparty to both sides of each trade. Central clearing allows dealers to net their positions against a single counterparty across many trades, substantially reducing gross balance-sheet exposures. Moreover, the CCP applies standardised risk-management tools, including initial and variation margin, and facilitates efficient price formation through anonymous order books. 8 The dealer-to-client segment, by contrast, is an over-the-counter (OTC) bilateral market. Because netting is only possible within each individual dealer–client relationship, gross exposures remain larger and balance-sheet constraints are more binding than in centrally cleared markets. There is no centralised price formation mechanism; instead, contract terms are negotiated bilaterally and are relationship-specific. The focus of this paper is on the bilateral dealer-to-client segment of the euro area money market, which provides a uniquely suitable setting to study how repo haircuts are set in collateral- and funding-driven environments. This segment is characterised by bilateral con- tracting, relationship-specific bargaining, and limited transparency, making market frictions particularly salient. Moreover, the dealer-to-client segment represents the primary channel

through which monetary policy is transmitted from regulated dealer banks to non-bank fi- nancial institutions, allowing us to study directly how regulatory constraints affect both con- 7The cash lender in a repo transaction becomes the legal owner of the collateral for the term of the repo, and may use it for example, to settle delivery obligations or to re-pledge in a subsequent transaction (Duffie, 1996). 8For cleared transactions, it is common practice to report a zero haircut because risk management is handled through the CCP’s initial and variation margin framework. Our focus on the bilateral segment avoids this con- found. See also Schaffner, Ranaldo, and Tsatsaronis (2019) for evidence on dealer trading patterns and home bias in the inter-dealer segment. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 11

tract design and policy pass-through. Overall, the bilateral dealer-to-client segment is a subset of the broader bilateral repo market, which itself accounts for a substantial share of euro-area repo activity (Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026). Funding-driven versus collateral-driven repos. A key distinction for this paper is between funding-driven and collateral-driven repo transactions. In a funding-driven repo, the initiating party seeks cash; in a collateral-driven repo, the initiating party seeks a specific security or, more broadly, eligible collateral. This distinction matters fundamentally for the economics of haircut-setting. In a funding-driven repo, the haircut protects the cash lender against the liquidation risk of the collateral in the event of borrower default. The cash lender, therefore, has an incentive to demand overcollateralisation, implying positive haircuts. In a collateral- driven repo, the haircut protects the collateral provider (the dealer) against the replacement risk of the security: should the cash lender default and fail to return the collateral, the dealer must repurchase it in the open market, potentially at a premium. The dealer, therefore, has an incentive to deliver less cash than the collateral is worth, implying negative haircuts. 3. Theoretical Framework We develop a bilateral bargaining model in which a dealer and a client jointly negotiate the haircut and the repo rate, matching the institutional structure of the euro-area bilateral dealer-to-client repo market segment. The model embeds three frictions in a single framework: dealer balance-sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. It applies to both the collateral-driven and funding-driven segments, recovers the textbook risk- management haircuts when the three frictions vanish, and shows how each friction shifts haircuts within each segment. 3.5. Framework commitment and residual rate adjustment The equilibrium in Proposition 1 treats (h, r) as jointly renegotiated on each trade. In practice, bilateral repo relationships are governed by master framework agreements, most commonly the Global Master Repurchase Agreement (GMRA), which specify haircut sched- ules at the dealer–client level and are refreshed at agreed intervals, typically quarterly. Each schedule indexes haircuts by collateral characteristics (issuer country, rating, maturity, size), and every trade evaluates the schedule at its own coordinates. Between refresh dates, the hair- cut at any given schedule row is effectively committed; only the rate is renegotiated on each trade. This institutional feature is compatible with our empirical strategy: the transaction- level heterogeneity we exploit reflects variation across schedule rows (different collateral) and across dealer–client pairs (different schedules), not trade-level renegotiation of a fixed schedule entry. Empirical Analysis In our analysis, we consider three main money-market frictions and their impact on repo hair- cuts: (i) dealer balance-sheet constraints, (ii) the convenience yield embedded in the collateral value, and (iii) client outside options. 5.1. Dealer balance sheet constraints The post-crisis leverage ratio (LR) regulation treats repo transactions asymmetrically. Lending collateral against cash in a collateral-driven repo extends the dealer’s balance sheet, whereas ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 30

lending cash against collateral in a funding-driven reverse repo does not. Because the cash received in a collateral-driven trade increases one-for-one with a more negative haircut, con- strained dealers can free leverage capacity by raising haircuts in the collateral-driven segment. Ranaldo et al. (2021) document a related asymmetry for repo rates around quarter-ends; we show that the same asymmetry operates on the haircut margin, and that it is present through- out the entire quarter rather than only at reporting dates. On June 28, 2021, the 3% LR requirement under the EU’s Capital Requirements Regulation II (CRR II) became a binding Pillar 1 obligation for all ECB-supervised banks. Article 429e permits netting of securities financing transactions only under narrow conditions, notably identical counterparties and settlement dates. Matched-book intermediation across different clients, therefore, expands gross exposure on both legs and directly consumes scarce leverage capacity. The effective date of the implementation was predetermined years in advance, the timing of the shock was, therefore, exogenous to contemporaneous conditions in the repo market. Cross-sectional dispersion in how close each dealer sits to the 3% threshold generates variation in treatment intensity. Euro-area banks must report both a point-in-time and an averaged version of the lever- age ratio, we, therefore, expect dealer banks to internalise the constraint in their day-to-day haircut setting throughout the quarter, not only around reporting dates. Cross-sectional dif- ferences in dealer balance-sheet capacity should, therefore, shape haircuts throughout the entire quarter.
