Bonds with higher convenience yields are scarcer and more valuable to market participants (Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012; Ballensiefen and Ranaldo, 2023), which makes them costlier to re-source in the case of counterparty default. Higher convenience yields therefore push haircuts down in the collateral-driven segment, as dealers demand more cash upfront to insure against this replacement cost. In funding-driven trades, by contrast, the dealer receives the bond from the client and holds it for the term of the repo. Because the dealer can rehypothecate the bond during that time, receiving a scarcer or more valuable bond is more profitable. Higher convenience yields therefore raise haircuts in the funding-driven segment: dealers require the client to post more collateral per unit of cash lent, allowing them to
accumulate more of the valuable bond. This sign flip reflects the fundamentally different economic role of the haircut in each segment. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 7

Third, we show that client outside options push haircuts in opposite directions across the two segments. In funding-driven trades, the client borrows cash from the dealer and posts collateral. The client prefers a lower haircut, as this means posting less collateral per unit of cash borrowed. Consistent with this, clients with a broader network of active dealer relationships negotiate systematically lower haircuts. In collateral-driven trades, by contrast, the client lends cash to the dealer and receives a specific security. The client prefers a higher haircut, as this means receiving more collateral per unit of cash lent. Consistent with this, clients with broader outside options negotiate systematically higher (less negative) haircuts. The same underlying client characteristic therefore pushes haircuts in opposite directions across the two segments. Overall, this result implies that haircut levels are relationship- specific and shaped by client outside options, rather than adjusting only to time-varying collateral risk. Building on these frictions, the model yields two testable predictions for repo rates in the collateral-driven segment: (i) constrained dealers exhibit higher repo-rate volatility, and (ii) they transmit ECB deposit-facility-rate changes less completely to their clients. We confirm both in the data. Funding-driven trades, in which dealer leverage constraints have no effect on the haircut, serve as natural placebos: rate volatility and pass-through in the funding-driven segment are unrelated to dealer leverage. These results suggest that post-crisis leverage- ratio regulation carries unintended consequences for monetary policy transmission, operating through the composition of the repo contract. In sum, we provide evidence that haircuts in repo markets are shaped by different fric- tions across collateral- and funding-driven segments. The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. After introducing the related literature, Section 2 describes the institutional setting. Section 3 develops the bargaining model and derives its haircut and rate predictions. Sec- tion 4

introduces our data, Section 5 tests the model’s haircut predictions on transaction-level data, documenting how the three frictions shape haircut design in the collateral-driven and funding-driven segments. Section 6 tests the model’s rate-level predictions on volatility and monetary policy pass-through. Section 7 concludes. Related literature. Our analysis mainly contributes to two strands of the literature. First, we add to work on haircut determination in bilateral repo markets. Dang, Gorton, and Holm- ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 8

ström (2011) argue theoretically that haircuts exist to make collateralised debt “information- insensitive.” A growing empirical literature, however, documents that trade-level haircuts in bilateral repo are systematically zero or negative across jurisdictions — Europe (Hermes et al., 2025a,b; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), the United States (Hempel et al., 2023; Bejarano et al., 2025; Kahn and McCormick, 2025; Cenicola et al., 2025), and the United Kingdom (Julliard et al., 2026). Recent contributions have advanced several explanations: competition among lenders (Bittner and Jank, 2025), excess balance-sheet capacity (Bejarano et al., 2025), portfolio-level margining that substitutes for trade-level haircuts (Hempel et al., 2023; Hill and Westphal, 2025; Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026), wrong-way-risk premia between bor- rower and collateral (Barbiero, Schepens, and Sigaux, 2024), and dealer market power over less-connected clients (Hau, Hoffmann, Langfield, and Timmer, 2021). We contribute several distinct channels in explaining these repo haircut patterns by sys- tematically distinguishing betweencollateral- and funding-driven repo transactions: the Basel III leverage ratio as a first-order regulatory friction shaping haircut design in the collateral-driven segment of the euro-area bilateral repo market. We further document the first systematic evi- dence of segment-level asymmetry: convenience yields and client outside options act in oppo- site directions across collateral- and funding-driven repos. These channels operate alongside, and are distinct from, the portfolio-margining channel documented by Panzarino and Spo- laore (2026) and the wrong-way-risk channel of Barbiero et al. (2024). Whereas Bejarano et al. (2025) document how the zero risk-weight of Treasury repo enables U.S. dealers to sup- ply leverage to non-bank clients through negative haircuts, we identify the opposite margin — the leverage ratio constrains euro-area dealers and pushes haircuts upward in collateral- driven trades. The paper also relates to work on collateral demand and specialness in repo markets (e.g., Mancini, Ranaldo, and Wrampelmeyer, 2016; Arrata et al., 2020;

Corradin and Maddaloni, 2020; Coen, Coen, and Hüser, 2024).6 Second, we add to the literature on monetary policy, financial regulation, and the trans- mission process (e.g., Duffie and Krishnamurthy, 2016; Drechsler, Savov, and Schnabl, 2017; Ballensiefen et al., 2023; Eisenschmidt et al., 2024). Post-crisis bank regulation has been shown 6Studies on safe-asset scarcity show that high-quality government bonds in Europe command convenience yields that translate into repo pricing (Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012; Ballensiefen and Ranaldo, 2023). Gorton and Metrick (2012) document how repo haircuts spiked during the 2008 financial crisis. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 9

to distort short-term funding markets: Ranaldo et al. (2021) document quarter-end window dressing by European banks around the Basel III leverage ratio, Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018) document persistent covered-interest-parity deviations attributable to bank balance- sheet constraints, and Eisenschmidt et al. (2024) show that dealer market power in OTC repo reduces policy-rate pass-through. We advance this literature on two dimensions. First, we show that the leverage ratio reshapes euro-area repo not only at quarter-ends but throughout the entire quarter, and that it operates through haircut design rather than only through rates. Second, we identify a distinct within-dealer-sector transmission channel: because constrained dealers cannot use haircuts as an adjustment margin, the shock is displaced onto repo-rate volatility and onto the pass-through of policy rates to non-bank clients. These findings res- onate with Duffie and Krishnamurthy (2016) and Drechsler et al. (2017) on the imperfect transmission of central-bank rates through frictions in intermediary balance sheets. Lastly, we develop a theoretical model that rationalises our empirical findings. Our frame- work is a bilateral Nash bargaining model in the spirit of Infante (2019), reflecting the OTC search-and-bargaining structure of the dealer-to-client segment (Duffie, Gârleanu, and Peder- sen, 2005). It jointly determines the equilibrium haircut and repo rate under dealer balance- sheet costs, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options, and is augmented with a framework-commitment refinement that delivers closed-form predictions for rate volatil- ity and monetary-policy pass-through. This complements existing theoretical work on hair- cuts as information-insensitive risk mitigants (Dang et al., 2011), on margin-driven ampli- fication of financial cycles (Geanakoplos, 2010; Brunnermeier and Pedersen, 2009), and on the intermediary-balance-sheet view of asset pricing (Adrian and Shin, 2010; He and Krish- namurthy, 2013), by embedding a specific regulatory friction — the leverage ratio — as a first-order determinant of equilibrium contract terms. 2. Institutional

background Repurchase agreement. A repurchase agreement, or repo, is a short-term secured financing transaction in which one counterparty sells a security (most commonly a sovereign bond) to another, with an obligation to repurchase it at a predetermined price after an agreed period. A repo contract is characterised by four key terms, each negotiated at the transaction level: ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 10

(i) the volume of cash exchanged, (ii) the repo rate, (iii) the specific security posted as collat- eral, and (iv) the haircut applied to the collateral. 7 The collateralised nature of repos means they serve a dual function: they provide a vehicle both for obtaining short-term funding and for sourcing specific securities. Euro area repo market structure. The euro area repo market comprises two broad segments: an inter-dealer segment, in which dealers trade with one another, and adealer-to-client segment, in which dealers intermediate trades with non-dealer institutions such as investment funds, hedge funds, money market funds, insurance companies, and pension funds. The inter- dealer segment is predominantly centrally cleared. Transactions in the inter-dealer market are executed on electronic platforms (such as BrokerTec, Eurex Repo, and MTS Repo) and novated to a central counterparty (CCP), which becomes the legal counterparty to both sides of each trade. Central clearing allows dealers to net their positions against a single counterparty across many trades, substantially reducing gross balance-sheet exposures. Moreover, the CCP applies standardised risk-management tools, including initial and variation margin, and facilitates efficient price formation through anonymous order books. 8 The dealer-to-client segment, by contrast, is an over-the-counter (OTC) bilateral market. Because netting is only possible within each individual dealer–client relationship, gross exposures remain larger and balance-sheet constraints are more binding than in centrally cleared markets. There is no centralised price formation mechanism; instead, contract terms are negotiated bilaterally and are relationship-specific. The focus of this paper is on the bilateral dealer-to-client segment of the euro area money market, which provides a uniquely suitable setting to study how repo haircuts are set in collateral- and funding-driven environments. This segment is characterised by bilateral con- tracting, relationship-specific bargaining, and limited transparency, making market frictions particularly salient. Moreover, the dealer-to-client segment represents the primary channel

through which monetary policy is transmitted from regulated dealer banks to non-bank fi- nancial institutions, allowing us to study directly how regulatory constraints affect both con- 7The cash lender in a repo transaction becomes the legal owner of the collateral for the term of the repo, and may use it for example, to settle delivery obligations or to re-pledge in a subsequent transaction (Duffie, 1996). 8For cleared transactions, it is common practice to report a zero haircut because risk management is handled through the CCP’s initial and variation margin framework. Our focus on the bilateral segment avoids this con- found. See also Schaffner, Ranaldo, and Tsatsaronis (2019) for evidence on dealer trading patterns and home bias in the inter-dealer segment. ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 11

tract design and policy pass-through. Overall, the bilateral dealer-to-client segment is a subset of the broader bilateral repo market, which itself accounts for a substantial share of euro-area repo activity (Panzarino and Spolaore, 2026). Funding-driven versus collateral-driven repos. A key distinction for this paper is between funding-driven and collateral-driven repo transactions. In a funding-driven repo, the initiating party seeks cash; in a collateral-driven repo, the initiating party seeks a specific security or, more broadly, eligible collateral. This distinction matters fundamentally for the economics of haircut-setting. In a funding-driven repo, the haircut protects the cash lender against the liquidation risk of the collateral in the event of borrower default. The cash lender, therefore, has an incentive to demand overcollateralisation, implying positive haircuts. In a collateral- driven repo, the haircut protects the collateral provider (the dealer) against the replacement risk of the security: should the cash lender default and fail to return the collateral, the dealer must repurchase it in the open market, potentially at a premium. The dealer, therefore, has an incentive to deliver less cash than the collateral is worth, implying negative haircuts. 3. Theoretical Framework We develop a bilateral bargaining model in which a dealer and a client jointly negotiate the haircut and the repo rate, matching the institutional structure of the euro-area bilateral dealer-to-client repo market segment. The model embeds three frictions in a single framework: dealer balance-sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. It applies to both the collateral-driven and funding-driven segments, recovers the textbook risk- management haircuts when the three frictions vanish, and shows how each friction shifts haircuts within each segment. A dealer d and a client c negotiate the contract (r, h) over collateral issued by country j. Let C and V denote the cash exchanged and the market value of the

collateral at inception. The haircut is defined as h ≡ 1 − CV , (1) so thath>0 corresponds to overcollateralisation of the cash lender and h < 0 to undercol- lateralisation. For ease of presentation, we normalise the trade size: collateral-driven trades ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 12

are normalised per unit of collateral ( V = 1), so the cash leg equals 1 − h; funding-driven trades are normalised per euro of cash lent ( C = 1), so the collateral posted equals 1/ (1 − h). 3.5. Framework commitment and residual rate adjustment The equilibrium in Proposition 1 treats (h, r) as jointly renegotiated on each trade. In practice, bilateral repo relationships are governed by master framework agreements, most commonly the Global Master Repurchase Agreement (GMRA), which specify haircut sched- ules at the dealer–client level and are refreshed at agreed intervals, typically quarterly. Each schedule indexes haircuts by collateral characteristics (issuer country, rating, maturity, size), and every trade evaluates the schedule at its own coordinates. Between refresh dates, the hair- cut at any given schedule row is effectively committed; only the rate is renegotiated on each trade. This institutional feature is compatible with our empirical strategy: the transaction- level heterogeneity we exploit reflects variation across schedule rows (different collateral) and across dealer–client pairs (different schedules), not trade-level renegotiation of a fixed schedule entry. Empirical Analysis In our analysis, we consider three main money-market frictions and their impact on repo hair- cuts: (i) dealer balance-sheet constraints, (ii) the convenience yield embedded in the collateral value, and (iii) client outside options. 5.1. Dealer balance sheet constraints The post-crisis leverage ratio (LR) regulation treats repo transactions asymmetrically. Lending collateral against cash in a collateral-driven repo extends the dealer’s balance sheet, whereas ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 30

lending cash against collateral in a funding-driven reverse repo does not. Because the cash received in a collateral-driven trade increases one-for-one with a more negative haircut, con- strained dealers can free leverage capacity by raising haircuts in the collateral-driven segment. Ranaldo et al. (2021) document a related asymmetry for repo rates around quarter-ends; we show that the same asymmetry operates on the haircut margin, and that it is present through- out the entire quarter rather than only at reporting dates. On June 28, 2021, the 3% LR requirement under the EU’s Capital Requirements Regulation II (CRR II) became a binding Pillar 1 obligation for all ECB-supervised banks. Article 429e permits netting of securities financing transactions only under narrow conditions, notably identical counterparties and settlement dates. Matched-book intermediation across different clients, therefore, expands gross exposure on both legs and directly consumes scarce leverage capacity. The effective date of the implementation was predetermined years in advance, the timing of the shock was, therefore, exogenous to contemporaneous conditions in the repo market. Cross-sectional dispersion in how close each dealer sits to the 3% threshold generates variation in treatment intensity. Euro-area banks must report both a point-in-time and an averaged version of the lever- age ratio, we, therefore, expect dealer banks to internalise the constraint in their day-to-day haircut setting throughout the quarter, not only around reporting dates. Cross-sectional dif- ferences in dealer balance-sheet capacity should, therefore, shape haircuts throughout the entire quarter. Convenience yields Having examined how dealer balance-sheet constraints shape haircuts, we now turn to the role of collateral characteristics. Assets used as collateral in bilateral repo differ substantially in their scarcity, specialness, and value to market participants. Because these characteristics affect the dealer’s risk exposure differently across collateral- and funding-driven trades, they should transmit into haircut design asymmetrically across the two segments. In the preceding analysis we examined how dealer’s balance-sheet constraints shape haircuts. Of course, client and

collateral characteristics should also matter. A large literature documents that investors pay a convenience premium for the safety and liquidity services embedded in high-quality assets (Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012; Gorton, 2017), and that this premium is reflected in repo rates (Duffie and Krishnamurthy, 2016; Ballensiefen and Ranaldo, 2023). Convenience yields vary across securities (driven by differences in issuer credit quality, re- ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 35

maining maturity, and benchmark status) and over time with the opportunity cost of holding money (Nagel, 2016) or macroeconomic uncertainty (Moreira and Savov, 2017). Yet, while the link between convenience yields and repo rates is well established, far less is known about how convenience yields affect the haircut margin. We argue that convenience yields should influence haircuts in opposite directions across the two segments. In a collateral-driven repo, the dealer pledges a specific bond in exchange for cash; if the counterparty defaults and fails to return the security, the dealer must repur- chase a potentially scarce asset in the open market. The higher the convenience yield on the pledged bond, the costlier this replacement and the greater the dealer’s incentive to protect herself by demanding a lower haircut, i.e., demanding more cash in return for the collateral pledged. In a funding-driven repo, the dealer receives the bond from the client in exchange for cash and holds it during the term of the trade. As legal owner, she can re-use the collateral by pledging it in another repo, delivering it against a short, or posting it as regulatory margin, and thereby captures a fraction of its convenience yield through rehypothecation. This makes higher-convenience-yield collateral more valuable to hold, giving the dealer an incentive to demand more of it per euro of cash lent, i.e., a higher haircut. A standard liquidation-risk channel, in which more liquid collateral is easier to sell at a smaller discount upon default, would push in the opposite direction, but we argue that the rehypothecation channel dom- inates in bilateral repo. Under this framework, we expect the convenience-yield effect to be negative in the collateral-driven segment through replacement-risk protection, and positive in the funding-driven segment through the rehypothecation channel. To test these predictions, we regress transaction-level haircuts on

an ISIN-level conve- nience yield measure. This is consistent with the replacement-risk channel: when the pledged bond carries a high convenience premium, the dealer demands more cash in return for parting with it, reflected in a lower haircut, so as to be better insured against the cost of replacing a scarce and valuable security in the event of counterparty default. In the funding-driven sample (Columns 5–8), by contrast, the convenience yield enters with a positive and highly significant coefficient. This sign flip contradicts the risk-management prior: safer, more valuable collateral should require less over-collateralisation, not more. The result points instead to a different economic channel: rehypothecation. Because the dealer be- comes the legal owner of the received bond for the term of the repo, they can rehypothecate it in ways that scale with its specialness: re-pledging it in a subsequent collateral-driven trade at the specialness premium, delivering it against a short position, or lending it in the securities- lending market. The higher the convenience yield on the received bond, the more profitable these re-use opportunities and the greater the dealer’s incentive to accumulate more collateral per euro of cash lent, which translates into a higher haircut. Our results seem to suggest that, in the funding-driven segment, the rehypothecation channel dominates the risk-management channel. 5.3. Client outside options A

third key friction in the bilateral money market arises from market power. Establishing and maintaining trading relationships in OTC markets is costly and time-consuming, limiting the number of dealer links that clients can form. As a result, dealer banks may exercise mar- ket power over their OTC counterparties (Eisenschmidt et al., 2024; Bittner and Jank, 2025). To analyze the impact of dealer market power on repo haircuts, we estimate transaction- ECB Working Paper Series No 3301 38

level panel regressions using both collateral-driven and funding-driven samples. We proxy a client’soutside options by the number of distinct dealers a customer has traded with over the previous twelve months, which captures the active trading relationships supported by master agreements and trading infrastructure. Working Paper Series 
When less is more: behavioral effects 
of CBDC holding limits 
 
Thomas Garcia, Claudia Lambert, 
Cosimo Pancaro, Claire Rimbaud, Alice Soldà 
Disclaimer: This paper should not be reported as representing the views of the European Central Bank 
(ECB). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the ECB.  
No 3300 / October 2026 

Abstract
Holding limits are a central design feature of proposed retail central bank digital currencies
(CBDC). While such limits mechanically prevent individuals from exceeding a maximum balance,
they may also generate behavioral responses whose directions are a priori unclear. We conducted
an incentivized online experiment with participants from four euro-area countries, exogenously
varying the presence and level of a holding limit to causally separate direct mechanical effects
from behavioral effects. We find that behavioral responses increase holdings of the means of
payment subject to the holding limit, consistent with an attraction effect. This effect is material
only when the limit is high enough. Enabling reverse waterfall —automatic conversion into this
limited means of payment— increases adoption while reducing holdings. These results suggest
that combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms can support CBDC use while
containing holdings, thereby helping to mitigate potential financial stability risks.
Keywords: CBDC, holding limits, digital currency, behavioral economics, experimental economics.
JEL codes: E42, C91, D14, E58.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
1

Non-technical summary
Several central banks are exploring the possibility of issuing a central bank digital currency (CBDC)
— a digital form of public money for everyday payments. The CBDC design needs to balance ease of
use with ensuring that it preserves financial stability. In response, most CBDC projects foresee the
introduction of a holding limit, which would cap the amount of CBDC that individuals could hold in
their digital wallets. At the same time, automatic funding mechanisms such as the reverse waterfall
functionality can allow individuals to make payments even when they do not hold sufficient CBDC,
potentially reducing the need to hold large CBDC balances.
While holding limits would mechanically restrict how much CBDC people can hold, they may also
have a behavioral impact. For example, some individuals may view the limit as a restriction of their
decision rights, decreasing the attractiveness of the CBDC. For others, instead, the limit can act as a
reference point, attracting CBDC holdings towards that value. Understanding these possible responses
is important to assess how much CBDC people would actually hold and thus anticipate its impact on
the financial system if such limits were introduced.
This paper investigates how holding limits influence individuals’ choices about how to allocate their
money between different payment instruments. In particular, it studies whether the introduction of
a limit changes individuals’ behavior beyond its direct mechanical effect. The analysis also provides
empirical evidence on the reverse waterfall functionality. This mechanism automatically converts funds
from a user’s commercial bank account into CBDC whenever the user needs to make a payment but
does not currently hold enough CBDC.
To disentangle the direct effect of the limit from its behavioral effects, the paper uses a controlled
online experiment with 761 participants from four euro area countries: France, Germany, Italy, and
Spain. In the experiment, participants made decisions about how to allocate tokens between two
means of payment, then faced automated sellers, and earned money if they held the means of payment
required by the seller. One instrument bears interest but is not always accepted, while the other pays
no interest, is always accepted for payments and could be subject to a holding limit. These differences
capture the essence of the differences between bank-card payment and CBDC, where the former can
be remunerated via a deposit account and the latter can be used for peer-to-peer payments. Our
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
2

identification strategy relies on comparing participants’ decisions in the absence and the presence of
a limit, and assessing whether the level of the limit affects these behavioral responses by comparing
decisions with relatively lower and higher limits. In addition, we investigate how the presence of a
reverse waterfall functionality affects individuals’ responses to these limits.
Our results show that holding limits can generate indirect behavioral effects. Participants whose
initial holdings are below the limit, and thus would be expected to keep the same allocation in the
absence of indirect effects, tend on average to increase their holdings when the limit is introduced.
Moreover, distinguishing between relatively lower and higher limits, we find that this increase in
holdings emerges only when the limit is higher due to an asymmetric impact of attraction and repulsion.
When the limit is lower, the opposing behavioral responses offset each other, leaving average holdings
unchanged. By contrast, when the limit is set at a higher level, the anchoring effect becomes stronger
while the negative reaction to the restriction becomes weaker. As a result, average holdings increase
after the limit is introduced with the higher limit.
Finally, we find that introducing a reverse waterfall functionality both increases adoption of the
limited means of payment and decreases the level of its holdings. This suggests that these kind
of automated funding mechanisms can allow individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of
CBDC without requiring them to hold large CBDC balances.
Overall, we provide the first evidence that combining holding limits with automatic funding mech-
anisms can support the use of CBDC as a means of payment while addressing concerns about potential
financial stability risks.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
3

1 Introduction
Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC) are digital forms of sovereign currency issued by the central
bank. Several central banks are currently designing retail CBDC to complement physical cash by
providing individuals with an additional state-backed means of payment (Illes et al., 2025). CBDC
would bring central bank money into the digital age aiming to support financial inclusion, protect
privacy, and make payments easier and more secure for all. They would complement banknotes and
coins, giving people an additional choice about how to pay. However, preventing users from storing
excessive amounts in CBDC is also important to avoid excessive outflows of deposits from banks,
preserving financial stability. To address this concern, central banks such as the ECB, the Bank of
England, the Bank of Canada or the People’s Bank of China are designing CBDC that would feature
a “holding limit” which would limit, at any point in time, the amount of CBDC that individuals
could hold in their digital wallet (Panetta, 2022; Demertzis and Mejino-L´ op
ez, 2024).1 In parallel,
several CBDC projects are considering automatic funding mechanisms which would allow users to
make payments in CBDC without maintaining large CBDC balances.
Motivated by this central feature of CBDC, this paper studies how imposing a holding limit on
a means of payment affects consumers’ liquid wealth allocation. Introducing a holding limit has an
obvious direct effect on individuals’ allocation decisions by preventing users from exceeding the limit.
In addition to this mechanical effect, holding limits can have indirect behavioral effects reflecting a
change in consumer attitudes toward the means of payment that can further affect holdings. The
direction of these indirect effects is a priori not clear. On the one hand, users may perceive a means
of payment associated with a holding limit as a less attractive solution, leading them to hold fewer
funds in CBDC than what is directly implied by the mechanical impact. Indeed, a limit can have an
aversive impact by reducing decision rights (e.g. Bartling et al., 2014). On the other hand, the holding
limit can act as a reference or anchoring point when individuals choose how much to hold, potentially
leading them to hold amounts close to the limit, whereas they might have held less otherwise (e.g.
Ariely et al., 2003; Abeler et al., 2011).2 Given that these effects are behavioral and real-world data
on CBDC holdings are unavailable due to the lack of a large-scale CBDC implementation, we use an
1Beyond CBDC, holding limits have also been considered for stablecoins (Bank of England, 2025).
2Furnham and Boo (2011) provide a literature review showing that the anchoring effect is one of the most robust
cognitive heuristics.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
4

experimental approach to assess whether indirect effects occur and, if so, to identify the direction of
their influence on holdings.
Despite the importance of understanding the impact of a holding limit on CBDC holdings, to date,
there is no paper explicitly dedicated to this question. Incentivized experiments on CBDC have focused
on different aspects of the introduction of a CBDC on individuals’ portfolio allocations including the
introduction of a new payment method (Arifovic et al., 2023), greater privacy compared with other
digital payment instruments (Borgonovo et al., 2021; Magin et al., 2026), the possibility of bearing
interest (Camera, 2024), and their digital nature relative to cash (Camera et al., 2016).3 However, they
do not address the role of the holding limit. 4 More closely related to our contribution, some studies
use surveys, which include questions on holding limits but do not experimentally manipulate either
the existence or the level of such limits. For example, van der Horst and van Gent (2025) conduct
a survey experiment on digital euro and find that, on average, participants consider e1,297 to be a
logical amount for a holding limit by directly asking for the amounts to participants. Bidder et al.
(2024) develop a quantitative macroeconomic model calibrated using survey data and show that the
introduction of a holding limit is a necessary condition for a CBDC to be welfare-improving. Even
closer to our study, Georgarakos et al. (2025) estimate in a survey experiment the causal effect of
holding limits ranging from e1000 to e120000 on the propensity to adopt the digital euro and the
amount allocated to it compared with other liquid assets. They find that higher holding limits tend
to increase amount allocated.
Our preregistered study contributes to the literature by causally assessing the overall impact of
the introduction of a holding limit on individuals’ portfolio allocation while disentangling its direct
mechanical effect from its indirect behavioral effects. To achieve this objective, we employ an online
incentivized experiment that exogenously varies both the presence and the level of a holding limit.
Specifically, participants face an allocation decision between two means of payment, first without any
holding limit, and subsequently with one means subject to a holding limit. The baseline (No Limit )
condition allows us to elicit individual behavior in the absence of constraints, which can then be
compared to the behavior under the imposition of a holding limit to identify causal effects. After the
3See Jiang (2020) for a comprehensive review of experiments on CBDC.
4A growing literature (Li, 2023; Lambert et al., 2024; Nocciola and Zamora-P´ erez,2024) also aims to quantify the
potential CBDC demand, which is a key variable to determine the economic and financial stability implications of its
introduction, using econometric techniques and counterfactual exercises.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
5

allocation choice, participants use allocated tokens in trading activities that generate monetary payoffs.
Our experimental design differentiates itself from previous survey-based experiments by incorporating
real monetary incentives, thereby mitigating potential biases commonly found in survey studies (e.g.,
social desirability bias, hypothetical bias, etc.; Camerer and Hogarth , 1999).
In addition, we investigate how the presence of a reverse waterfall functionality affects individuals’
responses to these limits. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study how individuals
respond to a CBDC associated with a reverse waterfall (R W) functionality, a key feature designed
to preserve CBDC usability while limiting holdings in, for example, the foreseen design of the digital
euro (ECB, 2024b).5 This functionality enables users to draw on funds from a linked commercial
bank deposit account automatically converting them into CBDC whenever the user’s CBDC balance
is insufficient to complete a payment. This functionality is designed to operate alongside holding limits,
allowing policymakers to constrain CBDC holdings without restricting the use of CBDC as a means of
payment. However, little is known empirically about how individuals would respond to such a feature
or about its effect on CBDC holdings. To address this gap, our experimental design includes a final
condition in which the reverse waterfall functionality is enabled in the presence of a holding limit.
Our subject pool consists of 761 individuals from the four most populous euro area countries—
France, Germany, Italy, and Spain—, all recruited via the online research platform Prolific. Sampling
potential future users of the digital euro across multiple countries enhances the external validity of our
findings for the euro area. 6
Our results highlight that holding limits can generate indirect behavioral effects, beyond their
mechanical role of capping maximum holdings. We find evidence of two opposing mechanisms affecting
the holdings of a substantial fraction of “unconstrained” individuals (i.e., those whose initial CBDC
holdings were below the limit). About 37% of them either increase (“attraction effect”) or decrease
(“repulsion effect”) their CBDC holdings once the limit is introduced and these effects cannot be
attributed to the mechanical impact of the limit. The overall net change thus depends on the relative
strength of each indirect effect, which appears to depend on the level at which the limit is set. Under the
5The term “reverse” is used to distinguish this mechanism from the “waterfall” functionality, which operates in the
opposite direction: CBDC is automatically transferred to bank deposits when incoming transfers cause holdings to
exceed the holding limit.
6The selection of these four countries reflects a trade-off between broad population coverage, as they account for more
than half of the euro area’s population, and practical constraints related to translating materials into multiple native
languages and the depth of available participant pools on Prolific.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
6

lower limit, attraction and repulsion offset each other, leaving the average holdings of the unconstrained
individuals unaffected. Under the higher limit, the repulsion effect is attenuated while the attraction
effect is strengthened, leading to a net increase in holdings of the limited means of payment among
unconstrained participants. Strikingly, when the limit is relatively high, the indirect behavioral effect
dominates the direct mechanical effect, resulting in higher average holdings of the limited means of
payment in the whole sample.
Finally, we show that introducing a reverse waterfall functionality increases adoption while reducing
average holdings. Thus, the waterfall can allow individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of
CBDC without requiring them to hold large CBDC balances. Taken together, these results highlight
the potential value of combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms to support CBDC
use while containing CBDC holdings.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: section 2 presents the experimental design,
section 3 reports the theoretical framework and hypotheses, section 4 presents the results and section 5
concludes.
2 Experimental Design
In our experiment, participants first allocate their tokens between two means of payment, then they
face automated sellers with whom they aim to complete trades. One means of payment, bank-card,
yields interests but is rejected by some sellers while the other one, CBDC, is universally accepted but
non-remunerated.7 The experiment follows a 3 × 2 design varying the presence of a limit and its level.
2.1 Characteristics of the means of payment
The characteristics of the two payment methods draw inspiration from key features of bank-card and
CBDC payments. However, they are not intended to replicate these payment methods in full detail,
but to introduce stylized comparative advantages to capture their essential characteristics while main-
taining a simplified structure that facilitates the understanding of the participants. Tokens allocated
7While neutral phrasing was used in the experiment presenting the two means of payment as payment A and payment
B, we refer to them using the name of the real-world instruments that inspired them. Accordingly, the remunerated
means is referred to as “bank-card” and the other one as “CBDC”.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
7

to bank holdings generate a 7% interest on all tokens allocated to this payment method, while CBDC
holdings are not remunerated. Thus, this reflects the opposition between a non-interest bearing CBDC,
such as the one envisaged in the euro area (ECB, 2025), and remunerated bank deposits. Bank-card
payments are only accepted by 90% of the sellers in the market, capturing the limited ability to make
peer-to-peer (P2P) bank-card payments. By contrast, CBDC payments are accepted by all sellers
reflecting the possibility to do P2P payments and legal tender status as envisaged, for example, by the
digital-euro design. 8 Furthermore, participants incur an entry cost of 0.5 tokens to allocate at least
1 token to their CBDC holdings, capturing the cost of transitioning to a new means of payment as
captured by, for example, Arifovic et al. (2023) and Magin et al. (2026). Finally, there is no limit on the
number of tokens that can be allocated to bank holdings, while the maximum number of tokens that
can be allocated to CBDC holdings can be limited. These characteristics are summarized in Table 1.
Model parameters were inspired by real-world values observed in the euro area but were primarily
chosen to ensure experimental salience and internal validity, given our focus on treatment comparisons
rather than individual decisions. The assumed 10% share of P2P payments is consistent with the
observed 6% share in the euro area in 2024 (ECB, 2024a). The 7% interest rate exceeds recent
remuneration on household deposits (e.g. the average household deposit rate in 2024 of 1.2% according
to MFI interest rate statistics). 9 This higher rate reflects the need to account for the smaller scale
of monetary amounts in the experiment relative to real life and to preserve strict monotonicity of
interest-generated gains once converted into fiat currency. 10

(Cipollone, 2025).
9In an experiment on CBDC, Choi et al. (2026) assume that credit card payments yield a 5% discount rate, whereas

ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
8

2.2 Stages, treatments and conditions
The experiment is composed of three conditions and two treatments. Each condition consists of two
stages: an allocation stage and a trading stage.
Allocation stage: Participants face an allocation decision in which they need to allocate their
endowment of 10 tokens between the two payment methods.
Trading stage: After their allocation decision, participants face 10 sellers with whom they can
“trade” in 10 successive rounds. Participants are incentivized to realize successful trades. 11 Require-
ments needed for a trade to be successful are varied between conditions.
Condition variations: As mentioned earlier, each participant faces three conditions during the
experiment (see Figure 1). In the No Limit condition, there is no limit on the number of tokens they
can allocate to their bank-card holdings. In the Limit and Limit & R W conditions, the number of
tokens that can be allocated to CBDC holdings is capped (the ceiling is varied between treatments).
In addition, the Limit & R W condition differs from the other two as regards the outcome of a trade
with a seller accepting only CBDC if the participant does not have tokens allocated to CBDC when
meeting the seller. In the No Limit and Limit, this trade fails. By contrast, in the Limit & R W
condition a token is automatically transferred from bank to CBDC holdings and is used to complete
the trade, providing that the participant has allocated at least one token to CBDC holdings in the
allocation phase. This latter constraint captures the need to have a CBDC account open to use the
reverse waterfall mechanism.
Treatment variations: There are two treatments, which are varied randomly at the subject level.
Each participant faces either a limit of 3 (Low Limit ) or of 8 (High Limit ) tokens in the Limit and
Limit & R W conditions.
11The interests generated from bank-card holdings and participants’ gains from trade are deposited on a separate
account and cannot be used to trade. The fixed cost associated with CBDC holdings is deducted from participants’
gains from trade at the end of the trading stage.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
9

Figure 1: Bet
ween-subjects treatments and within-subjects conditions
2.3 Experimen
tal procedures
The experiment was conducted online using the platform Prolific in November 2025. A total of 761
individuals participated from the four most populated euro area countries, namely France, Germany,
Italy, and Spain (190 participants per country except 191 for Spain; 374 in the Low Limit treatment
and 387 in the High Limit treatment). Instructions were provided in the native language of each
country (see English translation in Appendix E). The average age of the participants was 35 years old
(sd = 11) and 49.6% were female.
One condition, among the 3 conditions, was randomly selected for the payment. Each successful
trade yielded 10 points and points were converted at a rate of 50 points per £1.12 The bonus payment
was on average equal to £1.98. It adds to the hourly average payment of £2 (median time of 13
minutes) to constitute the total payoff per subject.
All participants faced the conditions in the same order: No Limit, Limit and Limit & R W. We
chose to position the No Limit condition first in order to have a benchmark allocation where the
potential implementation of a limit was unknown to the subject. Indeed, withdrawing the limit could
have affected allocations in a No Limit condition presented second thus preventing a clean estimation
of the impact of introducing a limit. Although this choice may introduce a potential order effect,
the design leaves little room for such effects to arise in practice, since we provided no feedback to the
subject until the payment screen was displayed at the very end of the session thus substantially restricts
opportunities for learning or strategic adjustment across rounds (see Carlsson et al., 2024 for similar
arguments). In order not to provide feedback during the trading stage, we asked participants to choose
12While all pa
rticipants were from euro area countries, the experiment utilized Prolific’s default currency.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
10

which means of payment to use if the seller accepted both means of payment and they had both types
of tokens available in conditions No Limit and Limit. This decision was then applied for all potential
transactions.13 In the Limit & R W, this decision was actually irrelevant as participants either: i)
allocated at least one token to CBDC and could complete all trades, ii) allocated all their tokens to
card-payment and thus could only pay with card, if accepted by the seller. Therefore, participants did
not have to make a choice in the trading stage of this condition.
At the end of the experiment, participants were asked to report their age, gender, native language
as well as their self-reported risk preferences (Dohmen et al.,2011). We also elicited how confident they
are in their ability to manage their finances using digital tools (such as online banking apps, digital
wallets, or investment platforms) and their preferred payment methods when paying for goods or
services in person (e.g., in stores) among cash, debit or credit card, a mobile payment app, or a digital
wallet (the exact instructions are reported in Appendix E). Finally, participants could rate the clarity
of the instructions and explain their allocation choices in each condition (open-ended non-mandatory
questions).
3 Framework and hypotheses
This section formalizes how the introduction of a limit on CBDC holdings affects individuals’ resource
allocation between CBDC and bank-card holdings. We distinguish between a direct mechanical effect
of the limit and two potential indirect behavioral effects: an attraction effect and a repulsion effect.
Based on this framework, we derive testable hypotheses.
3.1 Setup
Let xlC ∈ {0, . . . ,10} denote the number of tokens allocated to CBDC holdings by an individual in
condition C ∈ {N L, L, L&RW} and treatment with a limit l ∈ {Low, High}, whereN Ldenotes the
No Limit condition, L the Limit condition, and L&RW the Limit & R W condition, while Low and
13Designing the experiment to include ten consecutive decisions per subject could have offered a more intuitive task.
In such a setup, participants would have received information in each round about the seller’s type and hence about the
success of their trades. However, missed trades could have confounded subsequent allocation choices, while realizations
of sellers’ acceptance could have influenced their risk attitudes (Imas, 2016) or their expectations about future outcomes
(Chen et al., 2016). Given these limitations, and as decisions in this stage are not of particular interest to us, we chose
to favor a more constrained version of the decision set.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
11

High denote the limits in the corresponding treatments. An individual is characterized as an adopter
if xlC ≥ 1. We distinguish two types of individuals based on their allocation choice in the No Limit
condition. An individual is unconstrained by the limit if her No Limit allocation remains feasible once
the limit is introduced, i.e. if xlN L≤ l. In contrast, an individual is constrained if xlN L> l. In the
absence of indirect behavioral effects, standard revealed preference arguments imply that, on the one
hand, unconstrained individuals should not adjust their allocation when a limit is introduced, i.e.,
xlL = xlN Lif xlN L≤ l. On the other hand, and also due to the monotonicity of the objective function,
constrained individuals should allocate the maximum feasible amount to CBDC holdings, i.e., xlL = l
if xlN L> l.
3.2 Behavioral channels
We consider two indirect behavioral effects that may arise when a holding limit is introduced: a
repulsion effect and an attraction effect. To avoid possible confounds from the direct effect of the
limit, we focus our analysis on the allocation decisions of unconstrained individuals, for whom the
limit implies no direct effect and thus no change in allocation (x lL = xlN L). Therefore, any deviation
from this benchmark reveals the presence of an indirect behavioral effect.
The repulsion effect captures a reduced interest in the restricted means of payment. When a limit
is introduced, individuals may perceive the CBDC as less attractive and reduce their allocation relative
to the No Limit condition. This implies xlL < xlN L. In contrast, the attraction effect corresponds to an
anchoring of the allocation decision to CBDC holdings towards the limit l, increasing CBDC holdings
for unconstrained individuals. This implies xlL > xlN L.
Because individuals may be subject to both effects simultaneously, we interpret an overall decrease
in CBDC holdings (x lL < xlN L) as evidence of a dominant repulsion effect, and an overall increase in
CBDC holdings (x lL > xlN L) as evidence of a dominant attraction effect. When allocations remain
unchanged, behavior is consistent with the benchmark model without indirect effects or with offsetting
attraction and repulsion forces. 14
14Note that our identification of attraction and repulsion effects is intentionally reduced-form. We do not attempt to
structurally identify individual-specific behavioral parameters or to separately estimate the underlying attraction and
repulsion functions. Instead, we classify individual responses based on observed changes in CBDC allocations when a
holding limit is introduced.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
12

Hypothesis 1 (Response to the limit with indirect effects) For unconstrained individuals, the
introduction of a holding limit changes CBDC allocations: xlL − xlN L= 0.
A negative change indicates a dominant repulsion effect, a positive change indicates a dominant at-
traction effect, while no change is consistent both with offsetting attraction and repulsion forces or no
indirect effects.
The magnitude of indirect behavioral effects is expected to depend on the level of the limit. A lower
limit restricts decision rights more strongly and is therefore expected to generate stronger repulsion
effects. By contrast, a higher limit provides a higher salient anchor and is expected to generate stronger
attraction effects.
The definition of unconstrained individuals, xlN L≤ l, varies with the level of the limit. As a result,
individuals with allocations such that xlN L > Low but xlN L ≤ High are unconstrained under the
High Limit but constrained under the Low limit. This mechanically changes the composition of the
unconstrained group across limits and may induce selection bias when comparing changes in CBDC
allocations. To cancel out this bias, we evaluate the magnitude of indirect effects—and consistently
all between-limit comparisons—using decisions of ex-ante similar individuals under the High limit,
namely those whose No Limit decisions would also leave them unconstrained under the Low limit
(xlN L≤ Low).
Hypothesis 2 (Interaction with the limit level) For ex-ante similar unconstrained individuals,
the change in CBDC holdings induced by the introduction of a limit is increasing with the level of the
limit l. Formally, for two limits l ∈ {Low, High}, andHigh > Low: xHighL − xHighN L ≥ xLowL − xLowN L.
3.3 Reverse waterfall mechanism
We now investigate associating a reverse waterfall mechanism to the limit affects CBDC holdings. To
do so, we focus our analysis on comparisons between the Limit and the Limit & R W conditions. In
the Limit & R W condition, participants still face a limit on the number of tokens they can allocate
to CBDC holdings. However, if needed to complete the trade, one token is automatically transferred
from bank-card to CBDC holdings, provided that the individual allocated at least one token to CBDC
holdings in the allocation phase. This can have two distinct effects. First, allocating a single token
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
13

now completely removes the risk of failed transactions for the same cost as in the Limit condition,
increasing the likelihood of adoption (“adoption effect”). Second, conditional on adoption, allocating
more than one token no longer provides additional transactional benefits and entails an opportunity
cost in terms of foregone interest, leading to a reduction in the number of tokens allocated to CBDC
holdings (“intensive-margin effect”).
Hypothesis 3 (Response to the reverse waterfall mechanism) Given both the adoption and in-
tensity effects, the reverse waterfall mechanism induces individuals’ allocations to CBDC holdings to
converge toward 1: |xlL&RW − 1| < |xlL − 1|.
4 Results
We first describe the level of CBDC holdings in the No Limit condition. Then, we assess the impact of
introducing a limit by focusing on the difference between the No Limit and Limit conditions. Finally,
we investigate the impact of introducing the reverse waterfall functionality by comparing the Limit
and Limit & R W conditions. The analyses presented in this section are preregistered unless stated
otherwise.15 Finally, we briefly comment on the impact of the demographics on our main variables.
4.1 Descriptive statistics: CBDC holdings by condition
Figure 2 presents the distribution of tokens allocated to CBDC holdings in each condition. In the No
Limit condition, the CBDC holdings of the participants are on average 2.68 tokens, which are close to
the optimal holding of 3 tokens for a risk neutral individual suggesting that participants understood
the incentives of the task. 16 Mean holdings exhibit a reduction to 2.35 tokens in the Limit condition,
and decline further to 2.05 in the Limit & R W condition.
15The preregistration is available at https://osf.io/7wc3n. Note that we preregistered the statistical analysis to test
for the null hypotheses. All tests performed hereafter are two-sided tests.
16The optimal holdings of 3 tokens is obtained by maximizing expected payoffs, as detailed in Appendix A. This
prediction remains unchanged under a prospect-theory utility specification using standard parameter values such as
those estimated by Wu and Gonzalez (1996); Abdellaoui (2000); Abdellaoui et al. (2005) (value function curvature of
0.49 to 0.91 and weighting function parameter of 0.60 to 0.76).
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
14

Figure 2: Distribution of CBDC holdings in each condition
4.2 Overall effect of the limit
W
e start by assessing whether the responses of the unconstrained participants to the limit reveals the
existence of indirect behavioral effects. Unconstrained participants represent 71.4% (N= 267) of the
participants in the Low Limit treatment and 96.9% (N= 375) in the High Limit treatment.
Result 1 When a limit is introduced, unconstrained participants hold more CBDC.
Support for Result 1 : We find a significant difference in the amount of tokens allocated to CBDC
holdings by unconstrained participants between the No Limit and the Limit conditions, supporting
Hypothesis 1 (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p= 0.005, Figure 3a). This suggests the presence of be-
havioral effects. While introducing a limit reduces CBDC holdings overall, this amount increases on
average from the No Limit (mean: 2.04 tokens) to the Limit condition (mean: 2.23 tokens) for uncon-

4.3 Attraction & repulsion effects of the limit
To understand the mechanisms behind Result 2, we now explore the heterogeneity in individuals’
responses to assess the existence and magnitude of the attraction and repulsion effects for each limit. 20
We first focus on the repulsion effect. We assess whether some participants are subject to repulsion
and compare its magnitude between the Low Limit and High Limit treatment. We conduct separate
analyses for constrained and ex-ante similar unconstrained participants as repulsion does not have the
same consequences on both sub-samples. In the absence of indirect effect, constrained participants are
expected to reduce their CBDC holdings in the Limit condition to exactly match the limit. Any further
reduction can thus be interpreted as evidence of a repulsion effect. In the Low Limit treatment, CBDC
holdings of constrained participants is lower than 3 tokens (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p= 0.003, 71.0%
of the participants hold 3 CBDC tokens), while in the High Limit treatment CBDC holdings are not
statistically different from 8 tokens (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p= 0.35, 83.3% of the participants are
at 8 CBDC tokens). This provides some evidence of a higher repulsion effect of the lower limit among
the constrained participants.
Next, we focus on the ex-ante similar unconstrained participants who can reduce their amount of
CBDC held in the Limit condition compared to the No Limit condition (i.e. participants holding 1
to 3 CBDC tokens in the No Limit condition). We find that there are significantly fewer of these
participants who reduce their CBDC holdings in the High Limit treatment than in the Low Limit
treatment (respectively 12.9% vs 21.7%; proportion test, p-value=0.023, Figure 4a). Among those
reducing their holdings, the decrease is of comparable size in each treatment (-1.28 vs -1.30 tokens
respectively in Low Limit treatment and in the High Limit treatment; t-test, p= 0.89; Figure 4b).
Therefore, analyses on both constrained and unconstrained participants offer converging evidence of a
higher repulsion effect under the Low Limit treatment.
We now compare the attraction effect between the High Limit and the Low Limit treatments
by focusing on ex-ante similar unconstrained participants. These subjects can increase their CBDC
holdings between the No Limit and the Limit condition. These are participants who allocate between 0
and 2 tokens to CBDC in the No Limit treatment).21 We find that 23.7% of these participants increase

Result 3 Allocations converge toward holding one CBDC token when a reverse waterfall mechanism
is introduced.
Support for Result 3 : As can be seen in Figure 2, the proportion of individuals holding exactly

CBDC holdings of adopters. Regarding the former, the proportion of non-adopters is approximately

of adopters decrease from 2.76 to 2.24 tokens (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p< 0.001) as presented in
Figure 3b.24 Overall, we observe a decrease in CBDC holdings from 2.35 to 2.05 tokens in the Limit &
R W condition compared to the Limit conditions showing that the reduction of CBDC holdings among
adopters dominates the increase in adoption (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p< 0.001).

Limit or the Low Limit treatment.25 We further note that the reduction in mean CBDC holdings is

downward effect of the limit on holdings, it does not make it redundant. It thus confirms that the
reverse waterfall functionality is best to be used in combination with a holding limit.

4.5 Additional analysis: individual characteristics
We explore individual determinants of i) the CBDC holdings, and ii) the change in CBDC holdings
between the No Limit and Limit conditions.
Regarding the holdings, we regress the amount allocated to CBDC holdings on a set of control
variables, first focusing only on demographics, then adding either risk aversion or variables related to
payment savviness and, finally, by including all of these variables together (seeTable A-2 in Appendix).
All regressions include country fixed-effects and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. We find
that the more-risk averse individuals are, the more tokens they allocate to CBDC holdings. This is
consistent with bank-card holdings having a higher risk of adverse outcomes (i.e., meeting with sellers
who only accept CBDC). Male participants allocate, on average, about 0.5 less tokens to their CBDC
holdings.
We use a similar approach to study the change in CBDC holdings between the No Limit and Limit
conditions while adding as regressor CBDC holdings in the No Limit condition to control for initial
allocations (Table A-3 in Appendix). We find that individuals with a higher digital financial confidence
adjusted less their holdings. We also find that preferring cash is also associated with less adjustment.
5 Discussion and Conclusion
We study how imposing a holding limit on a means of payment affects users’ attitudes towards it. We
find that the imposition of a holding limit has both a direct mechanical effect, capping the maximum
holdings, and an indirect behavioral effect, which increases the holdings of the limited means of payment
of the participants whose initial balances were below the limit.
We interpret this outcome as due to an attraction effect of the limit: the limit acts as an anchoring
point that shifts allocations toward that value. Moreover, distinguishing between a lower and a higher
limit, we find that this increase in holdings emerges only when the limit is higher.
The asymmetry of the results under the lower and a higher limit originates from the coexistence of
two opposite indirect effects: the attraction effect described above, and a repulsion effect. The latter is
driven by the restriction of decision rights, which renders the limited means of payment less attractive.
Under the lower limit, these two effects offset each other, leaving the average allocation unchanged.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3300
21

By contrast, a higher limit attenuates the repulsion effect while strengthening the attraction, thus
shifting allocations toward higher values and generating a net positive indirect effect. Indeed, we find
that, under the higher limit, the indirect effect dominates the direct effect of truncating the upper part
of the decision set, resulting in higher average holdings of the limited means of payment, and thus a
reversal of the expected effect of the limit. Finally, we provide the first empirical evidence that the
introduction of a reverse waterfall functionality can successfully mitigate the behavioral responses to
the holding limits, thereby increasing the adoption of the limited means of payment while containing
holdings. These findings shed light on indirect behavioral effects that may arise from introducing a
holding limit on a CBDC. Our experiment contrasts two means of payment: one that yields interest on
holdings but has limited acceptance, and the other that is universally accepted but unremunerated and
subject to a holding limit. In this respect, the design captures the core trade-off between remunerated
bank deposits, allowing person-to-business (P2B) payments, and an unremunerated CBDC enabling
both P2B and P2P transactions. These are expected features of, for example, the digital euro.
While caution is warranted when generalizing our results, our findings suggest that, when a limit
is set sufficiently high, it may increase CBDC holdings among individuals who, in the absence of
any constraint, would otherwise have held balances below that limit. By contrast, a sufficiently low
holding limit tends, on average, to neutralize the behavioral indirect effects. As an exploratory exercise,
we provide an order-of-magnitude interpretation of our lower and higher limit levels to enhance the
practical relevance of our results. Using a back-of-the-envelope calculation, we match quantiles of
CBDC holdings in the No Limit treatment with estimated average digital euro holdings from a euro
area–wide survey (Garcia et al., 2026). We find that the implied lower and higher limits correspond
approximately to e1000 and e5000, respectively. Indeed, in our data, 71% of participants hold no more
than 3 tokens, which matches the estimated share of individuals holding less than e1000. Similarly,
96% hold no more than 8 tokens, aligning with the estimated share of individuals holding below e5000
in the estimated real-world distribution. 26 Under the higher holding limit of e5000, extrapolating our
experimental estimates suggests an increase in CBDC holdings of about 13% for the individuals whose
unbounded holdings would be below the limit.
26This correspondence is consistent with Kim et al. (2025) that estimate that, in South Korea, less than 7% of
individuals would be constrained with a holding limit equivalent to e3000. In our experiment, 6.5% of the participants
are constrained by a limit of 6 tokens.

Our resul
ts further suggest that the reverse waterfall functionality, which allows individuals to
benefit from the payment advantages of CBDC without necessarily holding any, is a particularly useful
policy tool. Setting the level of the holding limit primarily reflects a trade-off between usability and
financial stability: a higher limit enhances usability by allowing larger holdings, while a lower limit
reduces the potential impact on the banking sector by limiting CBDC holdings and, therefore, possible
deposit outflows from commercial banks. When used in combination with a holding limit, a reverse
waterfall mechanism increases CBDC adoption while simultaneously reducing average holdings, thereby
delivering gains on both sides of the usability–financial stability trade-off.

In this section, we assess the robustness of our results by examining each country separately. We
first discuss the direction and magnitude of the effects by country, and then turn to their statistical
significance.
Regarding Result 1, the difference in CBDC holdings between the Limit and No Limit conditions
for unconstrained participants is, in every country, consistent with the direction reported in Result 1.
The magnitude of this difference ranges from 0.16 in Italy to 0.23 in Spain, compared with a sample-
wide average of 0.19. Similarly, for Result 2, the difference between the High Limit and Low Limit
treatments in the change in CBDC holdings between the Limit and No Limit conditions of ex-ante
similar unconstrained participants is positive in all countries, thereby confirming Result 2 at the
country level. This effect varies from 0.26 in France to 0.59 in Germany, relative to a sample average
of 0.41. Finally, consistent with Result 3, the difference in CBDC holdings between the Limit & R W
and Limit conditions is negative in all countries. The magnitude of this effect ranges from -0.34 in
Spain to -0.69 in France, compared with a sample average of -0.43.
Statistical significance at the country level is naturally affected by the fourfold reduction in sample
size relative to the pooled analysis, which limits the power of country-specific tests. For Result 1,
p-values of Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing holdings in the No Limit and Limit conditions are
between 0.06 and 0.38. For Result 2, p-values of Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing change in
holdings of unconstrained participants for the High Limit treatment and 0 are between 0.05 and 0.51.
Finally for Result 3, the Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing absolute deviation from 1 in Limit
and Limit & R W conditions have p-value of at most 0.002. As an answer to the lack of power, we
complement previous analysis with tests on whether country-level effects differ from the overall effect
using Mann-Whitney tests. For Result 1, we find no statistically significant differences at conventional
significance levels (ES, p-value = 0.75; FR, p-value = 0.87; IT, p-value = 0.70 and DE, p-value =
0.59). The same holds for Result 2 (ES, p-value = 0.96; FR, p-value = 0.45; IT, p-value = 0.99 and
DE, p-value = 0.38) and Result 3 (ES, p-value = 0.35; FR, p-value = 0.11; IT, p-value = 0.68 and
DE, p-value = 0.81).
In conclusion, we find that country-level effect sizes are always in the same direction as the sample-
