fragmentos_texto.texto: Working Paper Series When less is more: behavioral effects of CBDC holding limits Thomas Garcia, Claudia Lambert, Cosimo Pancaro, Claire Rimbaud, Alice Soldà Disclaimer: This paper should not be reported as representing the views of the European Central Bank (ECB). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the ECB. No 3300 / October 2026

Abstract Holding limits are a central design feature of proposed retail central bank digital currencies (CBDC). While such limits mechanically prevent individuals from exceeding a maximum balance, they may also generate behavioral responses whose directions are a priori unclear. We conducted an incentivized online experiment with participants from four euro-area countries, exogenously varying the presence and level of a holding limit to causally separate direct mechanical effects from behavioral effects. We find that behavioral responses increase holdings of the means of payment subject to the holding limit, consistent with an attraction effect. This effect is material only when the limit is high enough. Enabling reverse waterfall —automatic conversion into this limited means of payment— increases adoption while reducing holdings. These results suggest that combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms can support CBDC use while containing holdings, thereby helping to mitigate potential financial stability risks. Keywords: CBDC, holding limits, digital currency, behavioral economics, experimental economics. JEL codes: E42, C91, D14, E58. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 1

Non-technical summary Several central banks are exploring the possibility of issuing a central bank digital currency (CBDC) — a digital form of public money for everyday payments. The CBDC design needs to balance ease of use with ensuring that it preserves financial stability. In response, most CBDC projects foresee the introduction of a holding limit, which would cap the amount of CBDC that individuals could hold in their digital wallets. At the same time, automatic funding mechanisms such as the reverse waterfall functionality can allow individuals to make payments even when they do not hold sufficient CBDC, potentially reducing the need to hold large CBDC balances. While holding limits would mechanically restrict how much CBDC people can hold, they may also have a behavioral impact. For example, some individuals may view the limit as a restriction of their decision rights, decreasing the attractiveness of the CBDC. For others, instead, the limit can act as a reference point, attracting CBDC holdings towards that value. Understanding these possible responses is important to assess how much CBDC people would actually hold and thus anticipate its impact on the financial system if such limits were introduced. This paper investigates how holding limits influence individuals’ choices about how to allocate their money between different payment instruments. In particular, it studies whether the introduction of a limit changes individuals’ behavior beyond its direct mechanical effect. The analysis also provides empirical evidence on the reverse waterfall functionality. This mechanism automatically converts funds from a user’s commercial bank account into CBDC whenever the user needs to make a payment but does not currently hold enough CBDC. To disentangle the direct effect of the limit from its behavioral effects, the paper uses a controlled online experiment with 761 participants from four euro area countries: France, Germany, Italy, and Spain.

In the experiment, participants made decisions about how to allocate tokens between two means of payment, then faced automated sellers, and earned money if they held the means of payment required by the seller. One instrument bears interest but is not always accepted, while the other pays no interest, is always accepted for payments and could be subject to a holding limit. These differences capture the essence of the differences between bank-card payment and CBDC, where the former can be remunerated via a deposit account and the latter can be used for peer-to-peer payments. Our ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 2

identification strategy relies on comparing participants’ decisions in the absence and the presence of a limit, and assessing whether the level of the limit affects these behavioral responses by comparing decisions with relatively lower and higher limits. In addition, we investigate how the presence of a reverse waterfall functionality affects individuals’ responses to these limits. Our results show that holding limits can generate indirect behavioral effects. Participants whose initial holdings are below the limit, and thus would be expected to keep the same allocation in the absence of indirect effects, tend on average to increase their holdings when the limit is introduced. Moreover, distinguishing between relatively lower and higher limits, we find that this increase in holdings emerges only when the limit is higher due to an asymmetric impact of attraction and repulsion. When the limit is lower, the opposing behavioral responses offset each other, leaving average holdings unchanged. By contrast, when the limit is set at a higher level, the anchoring effect becomes stronger while the negative reaction to the restriction becomes weaker. As a result, average holdings increase after the limit is introduced with the higher limit. Finally, we find that introducing a reverse waterfall functionality both increases adoption of the limited means of payment and decreases the level of its holdings. This suggests that these kind of automated funding mechanisms can allow individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of CBDC without requiring them to hold large CBDC balances. Overall, we provide the first evidence that combining holding limits with automatic funding mech- anisms can support the use of CBDC as a means of payment while addressing concerns about potential financial stability risks. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 3

1 Introduction Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC) are digital forms of sovereign currency issued by the central bank. Several central banks are currently designing retail CBDC to complement physical cash by providing individuals with an additional state-backed means of payment (Illes et al., 2025). CBDC would bring central bank money into the digital age aiming to support financial inclusion, protect privacy, and make payments easier and more secure for all. They would complement banknotes and coins, giving people an additional choice about how to pay. However, preventing users from storing excessive amounts in CBDC is also important to avoid excessive outflows of deposits from banks, preserving financial stability. To address this concern, central banks such as the ECB, the Bank of England, the Bank of Canada or the People’s Bank of China are designing CBDC that would feature a “holding limit” which would limit, at any point in time, the amount of CBDC that individuals could hold in their digital wallet (Panetta, 2022; Demertzis and Mejino-L´ op ez, 2024).1 In parallel, several CBDC projects are considering automatic funding mechanisms which would allow users to make payments in CBDC without maintaining large CBDC balances. Motivated by this central feature of CBDC, this paper studies how imposing a holding limit on a means of payment affects consumers’ liquid wealth allocation. Introducing a holding limit has an obvious direct effect on individuals’ allocation decisions by preventing users from exceeding the limit. In addition to this mechanical effect, holding limits can have indirect behavioral effects reflecting a change in consumer attitudes toward the means of payment that can further affect holdings. The direction of these indirect effects is a priori not clear. On the one hand, users may perceive a means of payment associated with a holding limit as a less attractive solution, leading

them to hold fewer funds in CBDC than what is directly implied by the mechanical impact. Indeed, a limit can have an aversive impact by reducing decision rights (e.g. Bartling et al., 2014). On the other hand, the holding limit can act as a reference or anchoring point when individuals choose how much to hold, potentially leading them to hold amounts close to the limit, whereas they might have held less otherwise (e.g. Ariely et al., 2003; Abeler et al., 2011).2 Given that these effects are behavioral and real-world data on CBDC holdings are unavailable due to the lack of a large-scale CBDC implementation, we use an 1Beyond CBDC, holding limits have also been considered for stablecoins (Bank of England, 2025). 2Furnham and Boo (2011) provide a literature review showing that the anchoring effect is one of the most robust cognitive heuristics. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 4

experimental approach to assess whether indirect effects occur and, if so, to identify the direction of their influence on holdings. Despite the importance of understanding the impact of a holding limit on CBDC holdings, to date, there is no paper explicitly dedicated to this question. Incentivized experiments on CBDC have focused on different aspects of the introduction of a CBDC on individuals’ portfolio allocations including the introduction of a new payment method (Arifovic et al., 2023), greater privacy compared with other digital payment instruments (Borgonovo et al., 2021; Magin et al., 2026), the possibility of bearing interest (Camera, 2024), and their digital nature relative to cash (Camera et al., 2016).3 However, they do not address the role of the holding limit. 4 More closely related to our contribution, some studies use surveys, which include questions on holding limits but do not experimentally manipulate either the existence or the level of such limits. For example, van der Horst and van Gent (2025) conduct a survey experiment on digital euro and find that, on average, participants consider e1,297 to be a logical amount for a holding limit by directly asking for the amounts to participants. Bidder et al. (2024) develop a quantitative macroeconomic model calibrated using survey data and show that the introduction of a holding limit is a necessary condition for a CBDC to be welfare-improving. Even closer to our study, Georgarakos et al. (2025) estimate in a survey experiment the causal effect of holding limits ranging from e1000 to e120000 on the propensity to adopt the digital euro and the amount allocated to it compared with other liquid assets. They find that higher holding limits tend to increase amount allocated. Our preregistered study contributes to the literature by causally assessing the overall impact of the introduction of a holding limit

on individuals’ portfolio allocation while disentangling its direct mechanical effect from its indirect behavioral effects. To achieve this objective, we employ an online incentivized experiment that exogenously varies both the presence and the level of a holding limit. Specifically, participants face an allocation decision between two means of payment, first without any holding limit, and subsequently with one means subject to a holding limit. The baseline (No Limit ) condition allows us to elicit individual behavior in the absence of constraints, which can then be compared to the behavior under the imposition of a holding limit to identify causal effects. After the 3See Jiang (2020) for a comprehensive review of experiments on CBDC. 4A growing literature (Li, 2023; Lambert et al., 2024; Nocciola and Zamora-P´ erez,2024) also aims to quantify the potential CBDC demand, which is a key variable to determine the economic and financial stability implications of its introduction, using econometric techniques and counterfactual exercises. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 5

allocation choice, participants use allocated tokens in trading activities that generate monetary payoffs. Our experimental design differentiates itself from previous survey-based experiments by incorporating real monetary incentives, thereby mitigating potential biases commonly found in survey studies (e.g., social desirability bias, hypothetical bias, etc.; Camerer and Hogarth , 1999). In addition, we investigate how the presence of a reverse waterfall functionality affects individuals’ responses to these limits. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study how individuals respond to a CBDC associated with a reverse waterfall (R W) functionality, a key feature designed to preserve CBDC usability while limiting holdings in, for example, the foreseen design of the digital euro (ECB, 2024b).5 This functionality enables users to draw on funds from a linked commercial bank deposit account automatically converting them into CBDC whenever the user’s CBDC balance is insufficient to complete a payment. This functionality is designed to operate alongside holding limits, allowing policymakers to constrain CBDC holdings without restricting the use of CBDC as a means of payment. However, little is known empirically about how individuals would respond to such a feature or about its effect on CBDC holdings. To address this gap, our experimental design includes a final condition in which the reverse waterfall functionality is enabled in the presence of a holding limit. Our subject pool consists of 761 individuals from the four most populous euro area countries— France, Germany, Italy, and Spain—, all recruited via the online research platform Prolific. Sampling potential future users of the digital euro across multiple countries enhances the external validity of our findings for the euro area. 6 Our results highlight that holding limits can generate indirect behavioral effects, beyond their mechanical role of capping maximum holdings. We find evidence of two opposing mechanisms affecting the holdings of

a substantial fraction of “unconstrained” individuals (i.e., those whose initial CBDC holdings were below the limit). About 37% of them either increase (“attraction effect”) or decrease (“repulsion effect”) their CBDC holdings once the limit is introduced and these effects cannot be attributed to the mechanical impact of the limit. The overall net change thus depends on the relative strength of each indirect effect, which appears to depend on the level at which the limit is set. Under the 5The term “reverse” is used to distinguish this mechanism from the “waterfall” functionality, which operates in the opposite direction: CBDC is automatically transferred to bank deposits when incoming transfers cause holdings to exceed the holding limit. 6The selection of these four countries reflects a trade-off between broad population coverage, as they account for more than half of the euro area’s population, and practical constraints related to translating materials into multiple native languages and the depth of available participant pools on Prolific. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 6

lower limit, attraction and repulsion offset each other, leaving the average holdings of the unconstrained individuals unaffected. Under the higher limit, the repulsion effect is attenuated while the attraction effect is strengthened, leading to a net increase in holdings of the limited means of payment among unconstrained participants. Strikingly, when the limit is relatively high, the indirect behavioral effect dominates the direct mechanical effect, resulting in higher average holdings of the limited means of payment in the whole sample. Finally, we show that introducing a reverse waterfall functionality increases adoption while reducing average holdings. Thus, the waterfall can allow individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of CBDC without requiring them to hold large CBDC balances. Taken together, these results highlight the potential value of combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms to support CBDC use while containing CBDC holdings. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: section 2 presents the experimental design, section 3 reports the theoretical framework and hypotheses, section 4 presents the results and section 5 concludes. 2 Experimental Design In our experiment, participants first allocate their tokens between two means of payment, then they face automated sellers with whom they aim to complete trades. One means of payment, bank-card, yields interests but is rejected by some sellers while the other one, CBDC, is universally accepted but non-remunerated.7 The experiment follows a 3 × 2 design varying the presence of a limit and its level. 2.1 Characteristics of the means of payment The characteristics of the two payment methods draw inspiration from key features of bank-card and CBDC payments. However, they are not intended to replicate these payment methods in full detail, but to introduce stylized comparative advantages to capture their essential characteristics while main- taining a simplified structure that facilitates the understanding of the

participants. Tokens allocated 7While neutral phrasing was used in the experiment presenting the two means of payment as payment A and payment B, we refer to them using the name of the real-world instruments that inspired them. Accordingly, the remunerated means is referred to as “bank-card” and the other one as “CBDC”. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 7

to bank holdings generate a 7% interest on all tokens allocated to this payment method, while CBDC holdings are not remunerated. Thus, this reflects the opposition between a non-interest bearing CBDC, such as the one envisaged in the euro area (ECB, 2025), and remunerated bank deposits. Bank-card payments are only accepted by 90% of the sellers in the market, capturing the limited ability to make peer-to-peer (P2P) bank-card payments. By contrast, CBDC payments are accepted by all sellers reflecting the possibility to do P2P payments and legal tender status as envisaged, for example, by the digital-euro design. 8 Furthermore, participants incur an entry cost of 0.5 tokens to allocate at least 1 token to their CBDC holdings, capturing the cost of transitioning to a new means of payment as captured by, for example, Arifovic et al. (2023) and Magin et al. (2026). Finally, there is no limit on the number of tokens that can be allocated to bank holdings, while the maximum number of tokens that can be allocated to CBDC holdings can be limited. These characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Model parameters were inspired by real-world values observed in the euro area but were primarily chosen to ensure experimental salience and internal validity, given our focus on treatment comparisons rather than individual decisions. The assumed 10% share of P2P payments is consistent with the observed 6% share in the euro area in 2024 (ECB, 2024a). The 7% interest rate exceeds recent remuneration on household deposits (e.g. the average household deposit rate in 2024 of 1.2% according to MFI interest rate statistics). 9 This higher rate reflects the need to account for the smaller scale of monetary amounts in the experiment relative to real life and to preserve strict monotonicity of interest-generated gains once converted into fiat currency. 10

2.2 Stages, treatments and conditions The experiment is composed of three conditions and two treatments. Each condition consists of two stages: an allocation stage and a trading stage. Allocation stage: Participants face an allocation decision in which they need to allocate their endowment of 10 tokens between the two payment methods. Trading stage: After their allocation decision, participants face 10 sellers with whom they can “trade” in 10 successive rounds. Participants are incentivized to realize successful trades. 11 Require- ments needed for a trade to be successful are varied between conditions. Condition variations: As mentioned earlier, each participant faces three conditions during the experiment (see Figure 1). In the No Limit condition, there is no limit on the number of tokens they can allocate to their bank-card holdings. In the Limit and Limit & R W conditions, the number of tokens that can be allocated to CBDC holdings is capped (the ceiling is varied between treatments). In addition, the Limit & R W condition differs from the other two as regards the outcome of a trade with a seller accepting only CBDC if the participant does not have tokens allocated to CBDC when meeting the seller. In the No Limit and Limit, this trade fails. By contrast, in the Limit & R W condition a token is automatically transferred from bank to CBDC holdings and is used to complete the trade, providing that the participant has allocated at least one token to CBDC holdings in the allocation phase. This latter constraint captures the need to have a CBDC account open to use the reverse waterfall mechanism. Treatment variations: There are two treatments, which are varied randomly at the subject level. Each participant faces either a limit of 3 (Low Limit ) or of 8 (High Limit ) tokens in the

Limit and Limit & R W conditions. 11The interests generated from bank-card holdings and participants’ gains from trade are deposited on a separate account and cannot be used to trade. The fixed cost associated with CBDC holdings is deducted from participants’ gains from trade at the end of the trading stage. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 9

Figure 1: Bet ween-subjects treatments and within-subjects conditions 2.3 Experimen tal procedures The experiment was conducted online using the platform Prolific in November 2025. A total of 761 individuals participated from the four most populated euro area countries, namely France, Germany, Italy, and Spain (190 participants per country except 191 for Spain; 374 in the Low Limit treatment and 387 in the High Limit treatment). Instructions were provided in the native language of each country (see English translation in Appendix E). The average age of the participants was 35 years old (sd = 11) and 49.6% were female. One condition, among the 3 conditions, was randomly selected for the payment. Each successful trade yielded 10 points and points were converted at a rate of 50 points per £1.12 The bonus payment was on average equal to £1.98. It adds to the hourly average payment of £2 (median time of 13 minutes) to constitute the total payoff per subject. All participants faced the conditions in the same order: No Limit, Limit and Limit & R W. We chose to position the No Limit condition first in order to have a benchmark allocation where the potential implementation of a limit was unknown to the subject. Indeed, withdrawing the limit could have affected allocations in a No Limit condition presented second thus preventing a clean estimation of the impact of introducing a limit. Although this choice may introduce a potential order effect, the design leaves little room for such effects to arise in practice, since we provided no feedback to the subject until the payment screen was displayed at the very end of the session thus substantially restricts opportunities for learning or strategic adjustment across rounds (see Carlsson et al., 2024 for similar arguments). In order not to provide feedback during the trading
stage, we asked participants to choose 12While all pa rticipants were from euro area countries, the experiment utilized Prolific’s default currency. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 10

which means of payment to use if the seller accepted both means of payment and they had both types of tokens available in conditions No Limit and Limit. This decision was then applied for all potential transactions.13 In the Limit & R W, this decision was actually irrelevant as participants either: i) allocated at least one token to CBDC and could complete all trades, ii) allocated all their tokens to card-payment and thus could only pay with card, if accepted by the seller. Therefore, participants did not have to make a choice in the trading stage of this condition. At the end of the experiment, participants were asked to report their age, gender, native language as well as their self-reported risk preferences (Dohmen et al.,2011). We also elicited how confident they are in their ability to manage their finances using digital tools (such as online banking apps, digital wallets, or investment platforms) and their preferred payment methods when paying for goods or services in person (e.g., in stores) among cash, debit or credit card, a mobile payment app, or a digital wallet (the exact instructions are reported in Appendix E). Finally, participants could rate the clarity of the instructions and explain their allocation choices in each condition (open-ended non-mandatory questions). 3 Framework and hypotheses This section formalizes how the introduction of a limit on CBDC holdings affects individuals’ resource allocation between CBDC and bank-card holdings. We distinguish between a direct mechanical effect of the limit and two potential indirect behavioral effects: an attraction effect and a repulsion effect. Based on this framework, we derive testable hypotheses. 3.1 Setup Let xlC ∈ {0, . . . ,10} denote the number of tokens allocated to CBDC holdings by an individual in condition C ∈ {N L, L, L&RW} and treatment with a

We distinguish two types of individuals based on their allocation choice in the No Limit condition. An individual is unconstrained by the limit if her No Limit allocation remains feasible once the limit is introduced, i.e. if xlN L≤ l. In contrast, an individual is constrained if xlN L> l. In the absence of indirect behavioral effects, standard revealed preference arguments imply that, on the one hand, unconstrained individuals should not adjust their allocation when a limit is introduced, i.e., xlL = xlN Lif xlN L≤ l. On the other hand, and also due to the monotonicity of the objective function, constrained individuals should allocate the maximum feasible amount to CBDC holdings, i.e., xlL = l if xlN L> l. 3.2 Behavioral channels We consider two indirect behavioral effects that may arise when a holding limit is introduced: a repulsion effect and an attraction effect. To avoid possible confounds from the direct effect of the limit, we focus our analysis on the allocation decisions of unconstrained individuals, for whom the limit implies no direct effect and thus no change in allocation (x lL = xlN L). Therefore, any deviation from this benchmark reveals the presence of an indirect behavioral effect. The repulsion effect captures a reduced interest in the restricted means of payment. When a limit is introduced, individuals may perceive the CBDC as less attractive and reduce their allocation relative to the No Limit condition. This implies xlL < xlN L. In contrast, the attraction effect corresponds to an anchoring of the allocation decision to CBDC holdings towards the limit l, increasing CBDC holdings for unconstrained individuals. This implies xlL > xlN L. Because individuals may be subject to both

effects simultaneously, we interpret an overall decrease in CBDC holdings (x lL < xlN L) as evidence of a dominant repulsion effect, and an overall increase in CBDC holdings (x lL > xlN L) as evidence of a dominant attraction effect. When allocations remain unchanged, behavior is consistent with the benchmark model without indirect effects or with offsetting attraction and repulsion forces. 14 14Note that our identification of attraction and repulsion effects is intentionally reduced-form. We do not attempt to structurally identify individual-specific behavioral parameters or to separately estimate the underlying attraction and repulsion functions. Instead, we classify individual responses based on observed changes in CBDC allocations when a holding limit is introduced. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 12

Hypothesis 1 (Response to the limit with indirect effects) For unconstrained individuals, the introduction of a holding limit changes CBDC allocations: xlL − xlN L= 0. A negative change indicates a dominant repulsion effect, a positive change indicates a dominant at- traction effect, while no change is consistent both with offsetting attraction and repulsion forces or no indirect effects. The magnitude of indirect behavioral effects is expected to depend on the level of the limit. A lower limit restricts decision rights more strongly and is therefore expected to generate stronger repulsion effects. By contrast, a higher limit provides a higher salient anchor and is expected to generate stronger attraction effects. The definition of unconstrained individuals, xlN L≤ l, varies with the level of the limit. As a result, individuals with allocations such that xlN L > Low but xlN L ≤ High are unconstrained under the High Limit but constrained under the Low limit. This mechanically changes the composition of the unconstrained group across limits and may induce selection bias when comparing changes in CBDC allocations. To cancel out this bias, we evaluate the magnitude of indirect effects—and consistently all between-limit comparisons—using decisions of ex-ante similar individuals under the High limit, namely those whose No Limit decisions would also leave them unconstrained under the Low limit (xlN L≤ Low). Hypothesis 2 (Interaction with the limit level) For ex-ante similar unconstrained individuals, the change in CBDC holdings induced by the introduction of a limit is increasing with the level of the limit l. Formally, for two limits l ∈ {Low, High}, andHigh > Low: xHighL − xHighN L ≥ xLowL − xLowN L. 3.3 Reverse waterfall mechanism We now investigate associating a reverse waterfall mechanism to the limit affects CBDC holdings. To do so, we focus our analysis on comparisons between

the Limit and the Limit & R W conditions. In the Limit & R W condition, participants still face a limit on the number of tokens they can allocate to CBDC holdings. However, if needed to complete the trade, one token is automatically transferred from bank-card to CBDC holdings, provided that the individual allocated at least one token to CBDC holdings in the allocation phase. This can have two distinct effects. First, allocating a single token ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 13

now completely removes the risk of failed transactions for the same cost as in the Limit condition, increasing the likelihood of adoption (“adoption effect”). Second, conditional on adoption, allocating more than one token no longer provides additional transactional benefits and entails an opportunity cost in terms of foregone interest, leading to a reduction in the number of tokens allocated to CBDC holdings (“intensive-margin effect”). Hypothesis 3 (Response to the reverse waterfall mechanism) Given both the adoption and in- tensity effects, the reverse waterfall mechanism induces individuals’ allocations to CBDC holdings to converge toward 1: |xlL&RW − 1| < |xlL − 1|. 4 Results We first describe the level of CBDC holdings in the No Limit condition. Then, we assess the impact of introducing a limit by focusing on the difference between the No Limit and Limit conditions. Finally, we investigate the impact of introducing the reverse waterfall functionality by comparing the Limit and Limit & R W conditions. 4.3 Attraction & repulsion effects of the limit To understand the mechanisms behind Result 2, we now explore the heterogeneity in individuals’ responses to assess the existence and magnitude of the attraction and repulsion effects for each limit. 20 We first focus on the repulsion effect. We assess whether some participants are subject to repulsion and compare its magnitude between the Low Limit and High Limit treatment. We conduct separate analyses for constrained and ex-ante similar unconstrained participants as repulsion does not have the same consequences on both sub-samples. In the absence of indirect effect, constrained participants are expected to reduce their CBDC holdings in the Limit condition to exactly match the limit. Any further reduction can thus be interpreted as evidence of a repulsion effect. In the Low Limit treatment, CBDC holdings of constrained participants is lower than 3 tokens (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p= 0.003, 71.0% of the participants hold 3 CBDC tokens), while in the High Limit treatment CBDC holdings are not statistically different from 8 tokens (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p= 0.35, 83.3% of the participants are at 8 CBDC tokens). This provides some evidence of a higher repulsion effect of the lower limit among the constrained participants. Next, we focus on the ex-ante similar unconstrained participants who can reduce their amount of CBDC held in the Limit condition compared to the No Limit condition (i.e. participants holding 1 to 3 CBDC tokens in the No Limit condition). We find that there are significantly fewer of these participants who reduce their CBDC holdings in the High Limit treatment than in the Low Limit treatment (respectively 12.9% vs 21.7%; proportion test, p-value=0.023, Figure 4a). Among those reducing their holdings, the decrease is of comparable size in each treatment (-1.28 vs -1.30 tokens respectively in Low Limit treatment and in

the High Limit treatment; t-test, p= 0.89; Figure 4b). Therefore, analyses on both constrained and unconstrained participants offer converging evidence of a higher repulsion effect under the Low Limit treatment. We now compare the attraction effect between the High Limit and the Low Limit treatments by focusing on ex-ante similar unconstrained participants. These subjects can increase their CBDC holdings between the No Limit and the Limit condition. These are participants who allocate between 0 and 2 tokens to CBDC in the No Limit treatment).21 We find that 23.7% of these participants increase 20Unlike the rest of our results, our analyses here were not pre-registered. 21We do not assess the presence of attraction on constrained participants as, by design, constrained participants cannot allocate more than the limit, which is the amount expected without indirect effect. The difference between these proportions is not statistically significant (proportion test, p=0.67). It means that, at the extensive margin, the attraction effect is similar with the lower or the higher limit. However, among those who increase their CBDC holdings, the intensity of the increase is stronger with the higher limit compared to the lower limit (mean increase of 2.60 vs 1.56, t-test, p-value= 0.005, Figure 4b). Result 3 Allocations converge toward holding one CBDC token when a reverse waterfall mechanism is introduced. Support for Result 3 : As can be seen in Figure 2, the proportion of individuals holding exactly one CBDC token — the theoretically-optimal allocation with the reverse waterfall 22 — rises from 19.8% to 44.8% in the Limit & R W compared to the Limit condition. In fact, one token becomes the most common allocation, although the average CBDC holdings remain statistically different from one (Mann-Whitney test, p < 0.001). Considering the entire sample, we find a convergence toward one in the Limit & R W condition compared to the Limit condition: the average absolute difference between CBDC holdings and one decreases from 1.65 to 1.21 tokens (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.001), thus supporting Hypothesis 3. This results both from i) an increase in CBDC adoption and ii) a reduction in CBDC holdings of adopters. Regarding the former, the proportion of non-adopters is approximately halved, from 14.8% in the Limit condition to 7.9% in the Limit & R W condition (McNemar test, p< 0.001, also presented in Figure 3b). 23. 4.5 Additional analysis: individual characteristics We explore individual determinants of i) the CBDC holdings, and ii) the change in CBDC holdings between the No Limit and Limit conditions. Regarding the holdings, we regress the amount allocated to CBDC holdings on a set of control variables, first focusing only on demographics, then adding either risk aversion or variables related to payment savviness and, finally, by including all of these variables together (seeTable A-2 in Appendix). All regressions include country fixed-effects and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. We find that the more-risk averse individuals are, the more tokens they allocate to CBDC holdings. This is consistent with bank-card holdings having a higher risk of adverse outcomes (i.e., meeting with sellers who only accept CBDC). Male participants allocate, on average, about 0.5 less tokens to their CBDC holdings. We use a similar approach to study the change in CBDC holdings between the No Limit and Limit conditions while adding as regressor CBDC holdings in the No Limit condition to control for initial allocations (Table A-3 in Appendix). We find that individuals with a higher digital financial confidence adjusted less their holdings. We also find that preferring cash is also associated with less adjustment. 5 Discussion and Conclusion We study how imposing a holding limit on a means of payment affects users’ attitudes towards it. We find that the imposition of a holding limit has both a direct mechanical effect, capping the maximum holdings, and an indirect behavioral effect, which increases the holdings of the limited means of payment of the participants whose initial balances were below the limit. We interpret this outcome as due to an attraction effect of the limit: the limit acts as an anchoring point that shifts allocations toward that value. Moreover, distinguishing between a lower and a higher limit, we find

that this increase in holdings emerges only when the limit is higher. The asymmetry of the results under the lower and a higher limit originates from the coexistence of two opposite indirect effects: the attraction effect described above, and a repulsion effect. The latter is driven by the restriction of decision rights, which renders the limited means of payment less attractive. Under the lower limit, these two effects offset each other, leaving the average allocation unchanged. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 21

By contrast, a higher limit attenuates the repulsion effect while strengthening the attraction, thus shifting allocations toward higher values and generating a net positive indirect effect. Indeed, we find that, under the higher limit, the indirect effect dominates the direct effect of truncating the upper part of the decision set, resulting in higher average holdings of the limited means of payment, and thus a reversal of the expected effect of the limit. Finally, we provide the first empirical evidence that the introduction of a reverse waterfall functionality can successfully mitigate the behavioral responses to the holding limits, thereby increasing the adoption of the limited means of payment while containing holdings. These findings shed light on indirect behavioral effects that may arise from introducing a holding limit on a CBDC. Our experiment contrasts two means of payment: one that yields interest on holdings but has limited acceptance, and the other that is universally accepted but unremunerated and subject to a holding limit. In this respect, the design captures the core trade-off between remunerated bank deposits, allowing person-to-business (P2B) payments, and an unremunerated CBDC enabling both P2B and P2P transactions. These are expected features of, for example, the digital euro. While caution is warranted when generalizing our results, our findings suggest that, when a limit is set sufficiently high, it may increase CBDC holdings among individuals who, in the absence of any constraint, would otherwise have held balances below that limit. By contrast, a sufficiently low holding limit tends, on average, to neutralize the behavioral indirect effects. As an exploratory exercise, we provide an order-of-magnitude interpretation of our lower and higher limit levels to enhance the practical relevance of our results. Using a back-of-the-envelope calculation, we match quantiles of CBDC holdings in the No Limit treatment with estimated average digital euro holdings

from a euro area–wide survey (Garcia et al., 2026). We find that the implied lower and higher limits correspond approximately to e1000 and e5000, respectively. Indeed, in our data, 71% of participants hold no more than 3 tokens, which matches the estimated share of individuals holding less than e1000. Similarly, 96% hold no more than 8 tokens, aligning with the estimated share of individuals holding below e5000 in the estimated real-world distribution. 26 Under the higher holding limit of e5000, extrapolating our experimental estimates suggests an increase in CBDC holdings of about 13% for the individuals whose unbounded holdings would be below the limit. 26This correspondence is consistent with Kim et al. (2025) that estimate that, in South Korea, less than 7% of individuals would be constrained with a holding limit equivalent to e3000. In our experiment, 6.5% of the participants are constrained by a limit of 6 tokens. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 22

Our resul ts further suggest that the reverse waterfall functionality, which allows individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of CBDC without necessarily holding any, is a particularly useful policy tool. Setting the level of the holding limit primarily reflects a trade-off between usability and financial stability: a higher limit enhances usability by allowing larger holdings, while a lower limit reduces the potential impact on the banking sector by limiting CBDC holdings and, therefore, possible deposit outflows from commercial banks. When used in combination with a holding limit, a reverse waterfall mechanism increases CBDC adoption while simultaneously reducing average holdings, thereby delivering gains on both sides of the usability–financial stability trade-off. Let k be the number of P2P transactions. k follows a binomial distribution: k ∼ Binomial(n, p) Card payments: We assume that individuals use card if card is available. We first compute the optimal strategy provided that a digital euro account is open ( x >0). The payoff raised by tokens allocated to CBDC is unchanged. D Robustness b y country In this section, we assess the robustness of our results by examining each country separately. We first discuss the direction and magnitude of the effects by country, and then turn to their statistical significance. Regarding Result 1, the difference in CBDC holdings between the Limit and No Limit conditions for unconstrained participants is, in every country, consistent with the direction reported in Result 1. The magnitude of this difference ranges from 0.16 in Italy to 0.23 in Spain, compared with a sample- wide average of 0.19. Similarly, for Result 2, the difference between the High Limit and Low Limit treatments in the change in CBDC holdings between the Limit and No Limit conditions of ex-ante similar unconstrained participants is positive in all countries, thereby confirming Result 2 at the country level. This effect varies from 0.26 in France to 0.59 in Germany, relative to a sample average of 0.41. Finally, consistent with Result 3, the difference in CBDC holdings between the Limit & R W and Limit conditions is negative in all countries. The magnitude of this effect ranges from -0.34 in Spain to -0.69 in France, compared with a sample average of -0.43. Statistical significance at the country level is naturally affected by the fourfold reduction in sample size relative to the pooled analysis, which limits the power of country-specific tests. For Result 1, p-values of Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing holdings in the No Limit and Limit conditions are between 0.06 and 0.38. For Result 2, p-values of Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing change in holdings of unconstrained participants for the High Limit treatment and 0 are between 0.05 and 0.51. Finally for Result 3, the Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing absolute deviation from 1 in Limit and Limit & R W conditions have p-value of

at most 0.002. As an answer to the lack of power, we complement previous analysis with tests on whether country-level effects differ from the overall effect using Mann-Whitney tests. For Result 1, we find no statistically significant differences at conventional significance levels (ES, p-value = 0.75; FR, p-value = 0.87; IT, p-value = 0.70 and DE, p-value = 0.59). The same holds for Result 2 (ES, p-value = 0.96; FR, p-value = 0.45; IT, p-value = 0.99 and DE, p-value = 0.38) and Result 3 (ES, p-value = 0.35; FR, p-value = 0.11; IT, p-value = 0.68 and DE, p-value = 0.81). In conclusion, we find that country-level effect sizes are always in the same direction as the sample- ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 32

ave rage effects. Using statistical tests that suffer from low power, we find that while effects are not always statistically significant at the country level, they are also never statistically different from the sample-average effects. We thus conclude that the evidence points toward the robustness of our results at the country level. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 33

texto:
This Time is Different: A Panoramic View of Eight Centuries of Financial Crises

This paper offers a "panoramic" analysis of the history of financial crises dating from England's fourteenth-century default to the current United States sub-prime financial crisis. Our study is based on a new dataset that spans all regions. It incorporates a number of important credit episodes seldom covered in the literature, including for example, defaults and restructurings in India and China. As the first paper employing this data, our aim is to illustrate some of the broad insights that can be gleaned from such a sweeping historical database. We find that serial default is a nearly universal phenomenon as countries struggle to transform themselves from emerging markets to advanced economies. Major default episodes are typically spaced some years (or decades) apart, creating an illusion that "this time is different" among policymakers and investors. A recent example of the "this time is different" syndrome is the false belief that domestic debt is a novel feature of the modern financial landscape. We also confirm that crises frequently emanate from the financial centers with transmission through interest rate shocks and commodity price collapses. Thus, the recent US sub-prime financial crisis is hardly unique. Our data also documents other crises that often accompany default: including inflation, exchange rate crashes, banking crises, and currency debasements.

Acknowledgements and Disclosures The authors are grateful to Vincent Reinhart, John Singleton, Arvind Subramanian, and seminar participants at Columbia and Harvard Universities for useful comments and suggestions and Ethan Ilzetzki, Fernando Im, and Vania Stavrakeva for excellent research assistance.
